Zero average charge also explains the absence of net charge-driven migration in an ideal electrophoresis experiment at the pI.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The amino acid carries a net positive charge: Below its pI, an amino acid has a positive average net charge because more of its ionizable groups are protonated. At the pI itself, the average positive and negative charges balance.

B. The amino acid carries a net negative charge: Above its pI, an amino acid has a negative average net charge because more groups are deprotonated. This differs from the zero average net charge at the pI.

D. All functional groups are uncharged: Charged groups remain present at the pI. For example, the predominant glycine zwitterion has –NH₃+ and –COO− groups whose charges cancel; neither group is uncharged.

Key Educational Points:

  • At the pI, positive and negative charges balance on average.
  • A zwitterion can contain charged groups while having zero net formal charge.
  • For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, pI is the average of the carboxyl and ammonium pKa values.

Bottom Line: pI is the pH of zero average net charge, not the pH at which every functional group is uncharged.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which type of bond links successive amino acid residues along a protein's polypeptide backbone?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: Peptide bond

Successive residues along a polypeptide backbone are joined by peptide bonds. A peptide bond is a covalent amide linkage running from the carbonyl carbon of one residue to the nitrogen of the next, formed between the α-carboxyl group of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the following one. Most peptide links are written –CO–NH–, but an internal proline residue has no N–H at that nitrogen.

Hydrogen bonds stabilize secondary structure. Ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and van der Waals forces contribute to tertiary structure. Disulfide bonds are covalent but link cysteine side chains rather than joining successive backbone residues.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Hydrogen bond: Hydrogen bonds help stabilize structures such as alpha helices and beta sheets. They are not the covalent C–N links that connect successive residues along the backbone.

B. Ionic bond: Attractions between charged side chains can stabilize protein structure, but they are not the amide bonds joining successive backbone residues.

D. Disulfide bond: Disulfide bonds connect the sulfur atoms of cysteine side chains. They can cross-link parts of a protein, but they are not the regular links between successive residues in the polypeptide backbone.

Key Educational Points:

  • A peptide bond joins a carbonyl carbon to the nitrogen of the next residue.
  • These bonds form the continuous polypeptide backbone.
  • Disulfide bonds link cysteine side chains rather than supplying the usual residue-to-residue backbone connection.

Bottom Line: Successive amino-acid residues are joined along the backbone by peptide bonds, which are covalent amide C–N links.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In a Fischer projection of a chiral α-amino acid drawn with COOH at the top and side chain R at the bottom, where is NH₂ for the L configuration?
options: Above the α-carbon in a Fischer projection
Below the α-carbon in a Fischer projection
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: Left in a Fischer projection

With COOH at the top and the side chain at the bottom of this Fischer projection, an L-amino acid has NH₂ on the left and H on the right. The D configuration has those horizontal positions reversed. The stated orientation is essential: 'left' alone does not identify configuration in an arbitrarily drawn projection. D/L describes configuration relative to a reference convention, not the sign of optical rotation. Glycine is achiral and is neither D nor L.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Right in a Fischer projection: With the stated top and bottom groups, placing NH₂ on the right gives the D configuration. D does not mean that the molecule must rotate light to the right.

C. Above the α-carbon in a Fischer projection: The top position is occupied by COOH in the projection specified in the stem. Placing NH₂ there would change the drawing convention, so the simple left/right rule would no longer apply as stated.

D. Below the α-carbon in a Fischer projection: The bottom position is occupied by the side chain R in the specified projection. It is not the NH₂ position for the L configuration.

Key Educational Points:

  • Use a defined Fischer orientation: COOH at the top and side chain R at the bottom.
  • In that orientation, NH₂ on the left gives L; NH₂ on the right gives D.
  • D/L does not specify the sign of optical rotation, and achiral glycine has no D/L designation.

Bottom Line: With COOH at the top and R at the bottom of the Fischer projection, NH₂ on the left identifies L. The orientation must be stated.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: An ideal α-helix has approximately how many amino acid residues per complete turn?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: 3.6 amino acid residues

The usual protein α-helix is a right-handed helical structure in which the polypeptide backbone coils around a central axis. Each complete turn of the ideal helix contains approximately 3.6 amino acid residues, with a pitch (rise per turn) of about 0.54 nm and a rise of about 0.15 nm per residue.

The helix is stabilized by a regular pattern of hydrogen bonds between the C=O group of residue i and the N–H group of residue i+4. The side chains project outward from the helix backbone. Proline and glycine tend to disfavor regular α-helical structure, proline because of its ring and glycine because of its conformational flexibility.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 2.5 amino acid residues: A value of 2.5 residues per turn does not describe the ideal alpha helix. Its approximate geometry is 3.6 residues per turn and a pitch of 0.54 nm.

C. 5.0 amino acid residues: Five residues per turn is not the standard alpha-helical value. Use approximately 3.6 residues per turn; actual protein helices can be distorted from the ideal geometry.

D. 7.2 amino acid residues: About 7.2 residues span two turns of an ideal alpha helix, not one. The one-turn value is approximately 3.6.

Key Educational Points:

  • An ideal alpha helix has approximately 3.6 residues per turn.
  • About 0.15 nm rise per residue gives a pitch of about 0.54 nm per turn.
  • Internal backbone C=O groups hydrogen-bond to N–H groups four residues farther along the chain.

Bottom Line: An ideal alpha helix has about 3.6 residues per turn and a regular i → i+4 backbone hydrogen-bond pattern.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Among the 20 standard amino acids in their free forms, which has a secondary α-amino group?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: Proline

In the unprotonated structure of free proline, the alpha-amino nitrogen is bonded to two carbon atoms and one hydrogen, making it a secondary amine. Its saturated ring joins the side chain back to that nitrogen. A secondary amine is not an imine, so 'imino group' is misleading here. When proline is an internal residue of a peptide, its nitrogen is part of a tertiary amide and has no N–H hydrogen-bond donor.

The ring restricts backbone rotation. Peptide bonds preceding proline have a higher cis proportion than most other peptide bonds, but most are still trans. Proline can introduce bends or kinks rather than necessarily destroying every regular secondary structure.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Glycine: Glycine is unique for having the simplest side chain (just a hydrogen atom), making it the smallest amino acid with no chirality at the α-carbon. However, free glycine has a standard primary alpha-amino group (-NH2), not a secondary one.

C. Tryptophan: Tryptophan contains a large aromatic indole ring system. Free tryptophan has a primary alpha-amino group like most standard amino acids, and its indole nitrogen belongs to that aromatic ring rather than to the alpha-amino group.

D. Histidine: Histidine contains an imidazole ring in its side chain, which has important acid-base properties (pKa ~6.0). Its imidazole nitrogens are part of that ring; free histidine's alpha-amino group is a standard primary amine. Only proline has a side chain that connects back to the alpha-amino nitrogen.

Key Educational Points:

  • Free proline's unprotonated alpha-amino nitrogen is attached to two carbons, so it is a secondary amine.
  • The ring connecting its side chain to that nitrogen restricts backbone rotation.
  • Once proline is an internal peptide residue, its nitrogen has no N–H bond for the usual backbone hydrogen-bond donation.

Bottom Line: Free proline has a secondary alpha-amino group, not an imino group. Internal peptide-bonded proline has a tertiary amide nitrogen with no N–H donor.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In the regular triple-helical regions of fibrillar collagen, which amino acid occurs at every third position?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: Glycine

Fibrillar collagen has a triple-helical structure of three polypeptide chains wound around each other. In its regular triple-helical regions the repeating motif is Gly–X–Y, with glycine at every third position. X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline; these are common occupants of those positions rather than requirements at every one.

Glycine occupies every third position of these regions because its side chain is only a hydrogen atom. At the tightly packed core of the triple helix there is room for little more, and a larger side chain would cause steric clashes. Certain glycine substitutions in type I collagen can disrupt the triple helix and cause osteogenesis imperfecta.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Alanine: Alanine is a small, nonpolar amino acid but is not the one required at every third position in collagen. The Gly-X-Y repeating motif specifically requires glycine because the interior of the collagen triple helix is so tightly packed that only glycine (with its single hydrogen atom side chain) can fit.

B. Proline: Proline often occupies the X position in the Gly-X-Y sequence, while hydroxyproline is common at Y. Glycine, rather than proline, is required at every third position in the regular triple-helical pattern.

D. Leucine: Leucine is a large, branched, hydrophobic amino acid that would be far too bulky to fit into the crowded interior of the collagen triple helix. The three polypeptide chains wind around each other so tightly that every third residue must be glycine, the smallest amino acid, to avoid steric clashes.

Key Educational Points:

  • The regular collagen triple helix contains a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence.
  • Glycine occurs every third position and fits into the tightly packed core because its side chain is only H.
  • Proline and hydroxyproline are common at X and Y positions, respectively.

Bottom Line: Regular triple-helical regions of fibrillar collagen follow a Gly-X-Y repeat. Glycine's small side chain allows close packing at the helix core.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of peptide bonds is classified as a:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: Hydrolase (protease)

Enzymes that hydrolyze peptide bonds are classified as hydrolases, specifically proteases (also called peptidases or proteinases). Hydrolases (EC class 3) catalyze bond cleavage in which water is consumed in the overall reaction.

Enzyme classMain reaction typeExample
Oxidoreductases (EC 1)Oxidation–reductionLactate dehydrogenase
Transferases (EC 2)Functional-group transferKinases
Hydrolases (EC 3)Hydrolytic bond cleavageProteases, lipases
Lyases (EC 4)Nonhydrolytic cleavage or addition across double bondsDecarboxylases
Isomerases (EC 5)Rearrangement within a moleculePhosphoglucose isomerase
Ligases (EC 6)Energy-coupled bond formation, often using ATPDNA ligase
Translocases (EC 7)Catalyzed movement of ions or molecules across membranesH+-transporting ATPase

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ligase: Ligases join molecules through energy-coupled bond formation, often using ATP. The reaction in the question instead cleaves a peptide bond by hydrolysis, so it belongs to the hydrolases.

B. Transferase: Transferases are classified by transfer of a functional group from a donor to an acceptor. The overall reaction here is hydrolytic cleavage of a peptide bond, which places the enzyme among hydrolases.

D. Lyase: Lyases catalyze nonhydrolytic bond cleavage or addition across double bonds. Some lyases can add or remove water, but that is different from hydrolyzing a peptide bond.

Key Educational Points:

  • Proteases, also called peptidases, are hydrolases in EC class 3.
  • Peptide-bond hydrolysis consumes water in the overall cleavage reaction.
  • The current enzyme classification has seven main classes, including translocases as EC 7.

Bottom Line: Proteases are hydrolases that cleave peptide bonds by adding water across the bond.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: What is the systematic IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. 2-methylbutane

The longest carbon chain has 4 carbons (butane). A methyl group (CH₃) is attached to carbon 2. For this singly substituted alkane, numbering from the end nearest the branch gives the substituent the lowest locant, yielding 2-methylbutane.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. 3-methylbutane: For this singly substituted butane chain, number from the end that gives the methyl group the lower locant. That gives position 2 rather than 3.

C. 2-methylpentane: 2-methylpentane would have a total of 6 carbons (5 in the main chain + 1 methyl branch). The given formula CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 has only 5 carbons total, so the longest chain is 4 carbons (butane), not 5 (pentane). Counting carbons carefully is essential for correct IUPAC naming.

D. isopentane: Isopentane is a common name for the same compound. The question specifically asks for the systematic name, which is 2-methylbutane.

Key Educational Points:

  • The molecule has five carbons in total, but its longest continuous chain contains four.
  • A methyl group on carbon 2 gives the systematic name 2-methylbutane.
  • Isopentane refers to the same compound by its common name.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which reagent is decolorized by ethene but not ethane at room temperature in the absence of ultraviolet light?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Bromine water

Bromine water loses its orange-brown color when bromine is consumed in reaction with ethene's C=C bond. Ethane does not produce this decolorization under the stated room-temperature conditions without ultraviolet light. This gives a visible distinction between these two hydrocarbons. Bromine decolorization is not uniquely specific to alkenes in every possible sample: other substances can also consume bromine.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Dilute NaOH: Dilute aqueous NaOH does not provide this color-change test for ethene versus ethane. NaOH is a strong base even when its solution is dilute; base strength and concentration are different properties.

C. Concentrated H₂SO₄: Concentrated sulfuric acid can react with ethene, so it could help distinguish this pair in a differently worded test. However, it is not the colored reagent that is decolorized in the reaction asked about here.

D. Anhydrous AlCl₃: Anhydrous AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid catalyst in reactions such as Friedel–Crafts chemistry. It does not provide the bromine color change described in the question.

Key Educational Points:

  • Ethene consumes bromine and decolorizes bromine water through reaction at its C=C bond.
  • Ethane does not produce the same change at room temperature without ultraviolet light.
  • A test's meaning depends on the substances and conditions: bromine can also react with compounds other than alkenes.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In the absence of peroxides, addition of HBr to propene produces mainly:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 2-bromopropane

Markovnikov's rule states that the hydrogen atom adds to the carbon of the double bond bearing more hydrogen atoms, while the halide adds to the more substituted carbon. In propene (CH₃CH=CH₂), the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate leads to 2-bromopropane as the major product.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 1-bromopropane: 1-bromopropane would be the anti-Markovnikov product, where bromine adds to the less substituted carbon. This occurs in peroxide-initiated (radical) addition of HBr. Under normal (ionic) conditions, Markovnikov's rule applies: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, and the halide adds to the more substituted carbon.

C. 1,2-dibromopropane: 1,2-Dibromopropane is the product expected when Br₂ adds across propene's double bond under suitable nonaqueous conditions. Adding HBr supplies one H and one Br, not two Br atoms.

D. 2,2-dibromopropane: 2,2-Dibromopropane contains two bromine atoms on the central carbon. A single HBr addition across propene's one double bond introduces only one bromine atom, giving mainly 2-bromopropane.

Key Educational Points:

  • Under ordinary ionic conditions, H adds to propene's terminal double-bond carbon and Br mainly to the middle carbon.
  • The major product is 2-bromopropane, consistent with formation of the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate.
  • Peroxides can change the mechanism and orientation of HBr addition, which is why the reaction conditions are stated.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The hybridization of carbon atoms in ethyne (C₂H₂) is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. sp

In ethyne, each carbon forms one triple bond (one σ and two π bonds) and one single bond to hydrogen. This requires two hybrid orbitals, corresponding to sp hybridization. The bond angle is 180°, giving ethyne a linear geometry.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. sp³: sp3 hybridization gives a tetrahedral geometry with four σ bonds and no π bonds. In ethyne, each carbon forms only two σ bonds (one C-H and one C-C) and two π bonds, requiring only two hybrid orbitals. The two unhybridized p orbitals form the two π bonds of the triple bond.

B. sp²: sp2 hybridization gives a trigonal planar geometry with three σ bonds and one π bond, as seen in ethene (C2H4). Ethyne has a triple bond requiring two π bonds, so carbon needs two unhybridized p orbitals. Only sp hybridization (two hybrid orbitals + two unhybridized p orbitals) satisfies this.

D. sp³d: In the usual hybridization model, each carbon in ethyne uses two sp orbitals for its sigma bonds and retains two unhybridized p orbitals for the two pi bonds. An sp³d description does not fit this carbon bonding arrangement.

Key Educational Points:

  • Each carbon in ethyne has two directions of sigma bonding and is described as sp-hybridized.
  • A carbon–carbon triple bond contains one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
  • Ethyne is linear, with bond angles of 180°.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which alkyne gives acetone (propan-2-one) on hydration with water, dilute sulfuric acid and a mercury(II) sulfate catalyst?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Propyne

Under these conditions, water adds to propyne to form an enol, CH₃C(OH)=CH₂. Proton transfer and rearrangement of the double bond then convert this enol into the more stable carbonyl compound, CH₃COCH₃, acetone. This enol-to-carbonyl change is called keto–enol tautomerism. The three-carbon skeleton is retained.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ethyne: Ethyne gives the enol CH₂=CHOH, which changes into ethanal, CH₃CHO. Ethyne has only two carbon atoms, so hydration cannot give the three-carbon product acetone.

C. But-1-yne: But-1-yne gives butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, under these hydration conditions. Its four-carbon skeleton is retained, so the product is not acetone.

D. But-2-yne: But-2-yne is a symmetrical four-carbon alkyne. Hydration and tautomerism give butan-2-one, the same ketone obtained here from but-1-yne, rather than three-carbon acetone.

Key Educational Points:

  • Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne first produces an enol that changes into a carbonyl compound.
  • Propyne gives acetone; count carbon atoms to check the product.
  • Ethyne gives ethanal, whereas both but-1-yne and but-2-yne give butan-2-one under these conditions.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: What is the product when 2-butene reacts with ozone (O₃) followed by reductive workup with Zn/H₂O?
options: 1 molecule of formaldehyde + 1 molecule of propanal
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. 2 molecules of acetaldehyde

Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond. 2-Butene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃) has the double bond between C2 and C3. Cleavage produces two fragments: CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde) from each side. Reductive workup with Zn prevents further oxidation to carboxylic acids.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. 1 molecule of formaldehyde + 1 molecule of propanal: 1 molecule of formaldehyde + 1 molecule of propanal would result from ozonolysis of 1-butene (CH2=CHCH2CH3), where the double bond is between C1 and C2. In 2-butene, the double bond is symmetrically placed between C2 and C3, so the cleavage produces two identical fragments (CH3CHO, acetaldehyde).

C. 2 molecules of formaldehyde: 2 molecules of formaldehyde would result from ozonolysis of ethene (CH2=CH2), where each carbon of the double bond has two hydrogens. For 2-butene (CH3CH=CHCH3), each carbon of the double bond bears a methyl group, yielding acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) rather than formaldehyde (HCHO).

D. 1 molecule of butanal: Butanal retains all four carbon atoms in one chain. Reductive ozonolysis of this acyclic alkene cleaves its central C=C bond, giving two molecules of ethanal instead. Cleavage of a cyclic alkene can leave both carbonyl groups in one molecule, so two separate products are not a universal rule.

Key Educational Points:

  • Reductive ozonolysis converts the two carbons of a C=C bond into carbonyl carbons.
  • Each double-bond carbon in but-2-ene bears a hydrogen, so the products are aldehydes.
  • One molecule of but-2-ene produces two molecules of ethanal, preserving the total of four carbon atoms.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: What is the conventional order used to outline the stages of a productive free-radical chlorination chain?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Initiation → Propagation → Termination

A radical chain is conventionally described as initiation, propagation and termination. Light can initiate methane chlorination by splitting Cl₂ into two chlorine radicals. During propagation, Cl· + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃·, followed by CH₃· + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl·. The regenerated chlorine radical can continue the chain. Termination removes radicals, for example when two Cl· radicals combine. These processes can occur at the same time in a reaction mixture; the sequence is a way of describing a productive chain.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Propagation → Initiation → Termination: Propagation requires radicals to be present. In the conventional description, initiation explains their formation before the chain-carrying propagation steps are introduced.

C. Termination → Propagation → Initiation: Termination describes removal of radicals, not their initial generation. Starting an outline with termination therefore does not describe how a productive radical chain is established.

D. Initiation → Termination → Propagation: Putting termination before propagation omits the repeated steps that produce chloromethane and regenerate a radical. An individual newly formed radical can nevertheless terminate without first propagating; the listed stages are not a compulsory timeline for every radical.

Key Educational Points:

  • Initiation generates radicals, such as by light-induced homolytic cleavage of Cl₂.
  • Propagation consumes a radical and generates another radical, allowing the chain to continue.
  • Termination removes radicals; it can occur while other chains are still propagating.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which factor helps explain why cyclopropane undergoes ring-opening reactions more readily than cyclohexane?
options: Its C–C bonds have significant angle strain
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Its C–C bonds have significant angle strain

The three-membered ring of cyclopropane forces its carbon framework into angles of about 60°, far from the preferred tetrahedral angle of about 109.5°. It also has torsional strain from eclipsing C–H bonds. Opening the ring can relieve this strain. Cyclohexane can adopt a chair conformation with bond angles close to tetrahedral and largely staggered bonds, so it has much less ring strain.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. It has fewer hydrogen atoms: Having fewer hydrogen atoms does not make a cycloalkane more reactive. Cyclopropane has 6 hydrogens (C3H6) compared to cyclohexane's 12 (C6H12), but the difference in reactivity comes from ring strain, not hydrogen count. The 60-degree bond angles in cyclopropane deviate enormously from the ideal sp3 angle of 109.5 degrees.

B. It has more π electrons: Cyclopropane has no pi electrons; it contains only σ bonds. Pi electrons are found in unsaturated compounds like alkenes and aromatic rings. Cyclopropane's high reactivity stems from the severe angle strain forcing its C-C bonds to bend, creating "banana bonds" that store extra energy and make the ring eager to open.

D. It is aromatic: Cyclopropane is not an ordinary aromatic π system. Its tendency to undergo ring opening is associated with ring strain, including angle and torsional strain, rather than aromatic stabilization.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cyclopropane has substantial angle strain because its ring angles are about 60°.
  • Eclipsing C–H bonds also contribute torsional strain.
  • Chair cyclohexane has much less strain; opening a strained ring can be energetically favorable.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following compounds has the highest normal boiling point, measured at 1 atm?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Cyclopentane

Cyclopentane has the highest normal boiling point in this set, about 49 °C. The approximate values for pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are 36, 28 and 10 °C, respectively. Among those three C₅H₁₂ isomers, greater branching is associated with weaker overall intermolecular attractions and a lower boiling point. Cyclopentane has the different formula C₅H₁₀, so that branching comparison alone does not establish its position. Molecular shape affects intermolecular interactions, but cyclic compounds do not universally boil above acyclic compounds.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Pentane: Pentane is the straight-chain C₅H₁₂ isomer and boils at about 36 °C. It boils above its two branched isomers, but below cyclopentane at about 49 °C.

B. 2-methylbutane: 2-Methylbutane is a branched C₅H₁₂ isomer with a normal boiling point of about 28 °C. It is therefore below both pentane and cyclopentane.

C. 2,2-dimethylpropane: 2,2-Dimethylpropane is the most compact of the three C₅H₁₂ isomers and boils at about 10 °C. It has the lowest, not the highest, boiling point in this set.

Key Educational Points:

  • Normal boiling points are compared at the same pressure, 1 atm.
  • Within the three C₅H₁₂ isomers here, increasing branching lowers the boiling point.
  • Cyclopentane boils at about 49 °C and has formula C₅H₁₀, not C₅H₁₂.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Treatment of propyne with sodium amide (NaNH₂) in liquid ammonia followed by methyl iodide (CH₃I) gives:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. But-2-yne

NaNH₂ is a strong enough base to deprotonate the terminal alkyne hydrogen of propyne (CH₃C≡CH), forming the acetylide anion CH₃C≡C−Na⁺. This nucleophile then undergoes SN2 reaction with CH₃I to give CH₃C≡CCH₃ (but-2-yne).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Butane: Butane (C4H10) is a fully saturated alkane with no triple bond. The reaction of a terminal alkyne with NaNH2 creates an acetylide anion (a carbon nucleophile), which then attacks methyl iodide in an SN2 reaction. This preserves the triple bond, so the product must be an alkyne, not an alkane.

B. But-1-yne: But-1-yne (CH3CH2C triple bond CH) would require adding an ethyl group to acetylene, not a methyl group to propyne. Starting from propyne (CH3C triple bond CH), the NaNH2 removes the terminal H to give CH3C triple bond C- Na+, which reacts with CH3I to give CH3C triple bond C-CH3 (but-2-yne), an internal alkyne.

D. Pent-2-yne: Pent-2-yne (CH3C triple bond CCH2CH3) has five carbons. Since propyne has 3 carbons and methyl iodide adds 1 carbon, the product can only have 4 carbons total. Carbon count is a quick way to eliminate wrong answers in synthesis problems.

Key Educational Points:

  • NaNH₂ removes the terminal hydrogen from propyne to form an acetylide ion.
  • The acetylide attacks methyl iodide by an SN2 reaction, forming a new C–C bond.
  • Adding one methyl carbon to three-carbon propyne produces four-carbon but-2-yne.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: For a planar, monocyclic, fully conjugated π system in its ground state, Hückel's rule predicts aromaticity when it contains:
options: Any even number of π electrons
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. (4n + 2) π electrons

Hückel's rule applies to a planar ring with a continuous set of overlapping p orbitals. A closed-shell system with 4n + 2 π electrons, where n is a nonnegative integer, is aromatic. The allowed counts begin 2, 6, 10 and 14. A planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n π electrons is antiaromatic. If a ring avoids planarity or lacks continuous conjugation, it may instead be nonaromatic. Electron counting alone is not enough.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 4n π electrons: A 4n π-electron count corresponds to antiaromaticity when the ring is also planar and fully conjugated. A nonplanar ring with that count, such as cyclooctatetraene, is nonaromatic rather than antiaromatic.

C. 4n + 1 π electrons: 4n + 1 is an odd number of pi electrons, which does not correspond to any standard aromaticity rule. Aromatic stability requires an even number of pi electrons following the (4n + 2) formula, where n = 0, 1, 2, 3... giving 2, 6, 10 and 14 pi electrons for a monocyclic ring. Benzene has 6, with n = 1.

D. Any even number of π electrons: Simply having an even number of pi electrons does not guarantee aromaticity. For example, cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons (an even number), but 8 does not fit the (4n + 2) formula. Instead, 8 = 4(2), making it anti-aromatic if planar. Cyclooctatetraene avoids this by adopting a non-planar tub shape.

Key Educational Points:

  • Apply Hückel's rule to a planar, cyclic, continuously conjugated π system.
  • The aromatic electron counts are 4n + 2, with n = 0, 1, 2 and so on.
  • A 4n count is antiaromatic only when the other structural conditions are met.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which substituent is an ortho/para director in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. -OH

The hydroxyl group (-OH) is an activating group that donates electron density to the ring through resonance (lone pairs on oxygen). This increases electron density at the ortho and para positions, directing incoming electrophiles there. -NO₂, -COOH, and -CHO are all electron-withdrawing and are meta directors.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. -NO₂: A nitro group withdraws electron density strongly through resonance and induction. It deactivates the benzene ring and favors meta substitution, unlike the activating hydroxyl group.

B. -COOH: A carboxyl group attached through its carbonyl carbon withdraws electron density from the aromatic ring. It is deactivating and meta-directing rather than activating and ortho/para-directing.

D. -CHO: The aldehyde group, –CHO, withdraws electron density through its carbonyl group. It deactivates the ring and favors meta substitution.

Key Educational Points:

  • A hydroxyl group can donate a lone pair into a benzene ring by resonance.
  • This donation activates the ring and favors substitution at the ortho and para positions.
  • –NO₂, –COOH and –CHO are deactivating meta directors in the examples here.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Nitration of benzene uses a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. The active electrophile is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. NO₂⁺

Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to generate the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺). This powerful electrophile attacks the electron-rich benzene ring in the rate-determining step of electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. NO₂⁻: NO2- (nitrite ion) is a nucleophile, not an electrophile. Electrophilic aromatic substitution requires an electron-poor species that attacks the electron-rich benzene ring. The nitronium ion (NO2+) is generated when concentrated H2SO4 protonates HNO3, causing it to lose water and form the powerful electrophile.

B. NO₃⁻: Nitrate, NO₃⁻, is the conjugate base of nitric acid. It is not the electrophile that attacks the ring in nitration. The active electrophile is the positively charged nitronium ion, NO₂⁺.

D. NO⁺: NO+ (nitrosonium ion) is an electrophile but is involved in nitrosation reactions, not nitration. Nitrosation typically occurs with nitrous acid (HNO2) and is important in diazonium salt formation from amines. The nitration of benzene specifically uses the nitronium ion NO2+, which adds -NO2 to the ring.

Key Educational Points:

  • The electrophile in standard mixed-acid nitration is NO₂⁺, the nitronium ion.
  • Sulfuric acid helps generate NO₂⁺ from nitric acid.
  • Nitration replaces a ring hydrogen with –NO₂ and restores aromaticity after the substitution.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Toluene undergoes electrophilic bromination faster than benzene because the methyl group is:
options: An electron-donating group by hyperconjugation and induction
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. An electron-donating group by hyperconjugation and induction

The methyl group donates electron density to the benzene ring through both positive inductive effect (+I) and hyperconjugation. This increases the electron density of the ring, making it more nucleophilic and thus more reactive toward electrophiles. The methyl group is an activating, ortho/para-directing substituent.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An electron-withdrawing group by induction: A methyl group is treated as electron-donating in this aromatic-substitution comparison. Its inductive effect and hyperconjugation help stabilize the positively charged reaction intermediate; it does not deactivate the ring by withdrawing electron density.

C. A meta director: A meta director directs incoming electrophiles preferentially to the meta position. Electron-withdrawing groups like -NO2, -CN, and -COOH are meta directors. The methyl group, being electron-donating, is an ortho/para director. It activates the ortho and para positions by increasing electron density at those sites through hyperconjugation.

D. A deactivating substituent: The methyl group activates the aromatic ring toward electrophilic bromination compared with benzene. It also favors ortho and para substitution. Activation describes the effect on reaction rate; directing describes the preferred position.

Key Educational Points:

  • A methyl substituent activates benzene toward electrophilic aromatic substitution.
  • Hyperconjugation and electron donation help stabilize the reaction intermediate.
  • Methyl is an ortho/para director; rate effects and positional effects are related but distinct ideas.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: What is the initial monosubstitution product when benzene reacts with CH₃Cl in the presence of AlCl₃?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Toluene

This Friedel-Crafts alkylation replaces a hydrogen on benzene with a methyl group, giving toluene. AlCl₃ acts as a Lewis acid and activates CH₃Cl by strongly polarizing its C–Cl bond. The ring attacks the activated methyl group; a freely existing methyl carbocation need not be invoked. Toluene is more reactive than benzene toward further alkylation, so additional substitution can occur if conditions allow it.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Chlorobenzene: Chlorobenzene results from introducing chlorine onto the ring, for example with Cl₂ and a suitable Lewis acid. CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ transfers a methyl group in this reaction; it does not chlorinate benzene.

C. Benzaldehyde: Benzaldehyde contains a formyl group, –CHO, but this reaction introduces –CH₃. A different formylation method is needed to introduce –CHO; formyl chloride is unstable and is not used like an ordinary acyl chloride.

D. Phenol: Phenol contains an –OH group attached directly to the ring. Neither CH₃Cl nor AlCl₃ supplies an oxygen-containing group in this reaction, so phenol is not the product.

Key Educational Points:

  • Friedel-Crafts alkylation forms a bond between an aromatic ring and an alkyl group.
  • AlCl₃ activates the alkyl halide; methylation does not require a free CH₃⁺ intermediate.
  • Toluene is the first product here, but its activated ring can undergo further alkylation.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which compound is NOT aromatic?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cyclooctatetraene

Cyclooctatetraene (COT) has 8 π electrons (4n where n = 2), which makes it anti-aromatic if planar. To avoid anti-aromaticity, COT adopts a non-planar tub-shaped conformation and behaves as a non-aromatic polyene. Pyridine, furan, and thiophene are all aromatic heterocycles with 6 π electrons.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Pyridine: Pyridine has six π electrons in its aromatic ring. Its nitrogen contributes one electron from a p orbital; the nitrogen lone pair lies outside the aromatic π system and is not part of that six-electron count.

C. Furan: Furan has four π electrons from its two double bonds and two from one oxygen lone pair. The resulting six-electron conjugated ring is aromatic.

D. Thiophene: Thiophene has four π electrons from its two double bonds and two from one sulfur lone pair. This gives an aromatic six-electron π system.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cyclooctatetraene adopts a nonplanar shape and is nonaromatic.
  • A planar, fully conjugated eight-π-electron ring would be antiaromatic.
  • Pyridine, furan and thiophene each have six aromatic π electrons, but their lone pairs contribute differently.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: During mononitration of chlorobenzene, which product or product mixture is formed preferentially?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. o- and p-nitrochlorobenzene

Chlorine is an ortho/para director despite being a ring deactivator. Although Cl withdraws electron density through its inductive effect (-I), it donates electron density through resonance (+M) from its lone pairs. The resonance effect selectively stabilizes the intermediate arenium ion at ortho and para positions. The principal products are the ortho and para isomers; this does not mean that no meta product can form.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. m-nitrochlorobenzene: m-nitrochlorobenzene would be the major product if chlorine were a meta director. However, chlorine is an ortho/para director (despite being a ring deactivator). Chlorine has lone pairs that donate electron density to the ring by resonance, favoring ortho and para positions, even though its inductive effect is electron-withdrawing.

C. 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene: 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene contains two nitro groups. The question specifies mononitration, which introduces one nitro group. Further nitration requires a separate reaction of the already deactivated nitrochlorobenzene.

D. Nitrobenzene: Nitrobenzene lacks the chlorine substituent. In the electrophilic nitration described here, a ring hydrogen is replaced by –NO₂ while the original chlorine remains attached.

Key Educational Points:

  • Chlorine deactivates a benzene ring overall through its electron-withdrawing inductive effect.
  • Lone-pair donation favors ortho and para substitution despite that deactivation.
  • Mononitration introduces one nitro group and retains the chlorine substituent.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons has 10 π electrons?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Naphthalene

Naphthalene, C₁₀H₈, has two fused six-membered rings and ten sp² carbon atoms. Each contributes one electron to its delocalized π system, giving ten π electrons in total. The shared ring atoms are counted only once. Benzene has six π electrons; anthracene and phenanthrene each have fourteen.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Benzene: Benzene has one six-membered ring and six π electrons. It is aromatic, but it is neither polycyclic nor a ten-π-electron system.

C. Anthracene: Anthracene has three linearly fused rings and fourteen π electrons. Counting its fourteen sp² carbon atoms gives the total without double-counting shared ring edges.

D. Phenanthrene: Phenanthrene has three angularly fused rings and fourteen π electrons. Its different arrangement of rings does not change that electron count to ten.

Key Educational Points:

  • Naphthalene contains ten π electrons distributed over a fused aromatic system.
  • Shared atoms in fused rings must not be counted twice.
  • Anthracene and phenanthrene have different ring arrangements but each contains fourteen π electrons.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
options: Phenol has a higher molecular weight
The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance with the benzene ring
The O–H bond in phenol is shorter
The ethyl group stabilizes ethoxide by withdrawing electron density
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance with the benzene ring

When phenol loses a proton, the resulting phenoxide ion (C₆H₅O−) delocalizes the negative charge into the aromatic ring through resonance, stabilizing the conjugate base. Ethoxide cannot do this, so ethanol is a much weaker acid (pKₐ ≈ 16 vs. phenol pKₐ ≈ 10).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Phenol has a higher molecular weight: Molecular weight has no direct relationship to acidity. Acidity depends on how well the conjugate base is stabilized after losing a proton. Phenol (MW 94) is more acidic than ethanol (MW 46) not because it is heavier, but because the phenoxide ion (C6H5O-) is resonance-stabilized by the benzene ring.

C. The O–H bond in phenol is shorter: A claim about a shorter O–H bond does not establish the relative acidity. This comparison concerns proton loss and the relative stabilization of the resulting conjugate bases; phenoxide has resonance delocalization that ethoxide lacks.

D. The ethyl group stabilizes ethoxide by withdrawing electron density: The ethyl group is electron-donating in this comparison, not an electron-withdrawing group that stabilizes ethoxide. The most useful distinction is that phenoxide can delocalize negative charge into the ring, whereas ethoxide cannot.

Key Educational Points:

  • Acid strength is related to the stability of the conjugate base produced by proton loss.
  • Phenoxide is resonance-stabilized; ethoxide lacks comparable resonance delocalization.
  • The approximate aqueous pKₐ values, 10 for phenol and 16 for ethanol, show that phenol is much more acidic.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Benzene reacts with acetyl chloride (CH₃COCl) in the presence of AlCl₃ to give:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Acetophenone

AlCl₃ activates acetyl chloride to form an acylium electrophile, CH₃CO⁺. Benzene reacts with this electrophile, and aqueous work-up releases acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃. The introduced carbonyl group deactivates the ring, so further Friedel-Crafts acylation is strongly disfavored. The resonance-stabilized acylium ion also avoids the carbocation rearrangements associated with some alkylations.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Toluene: Toluene (methylbenzene) is the product of Friedel-Crafts alkylation with CH3Cl/AlCl3, not acylation. Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride (RCOCl) and introduces a C=O-containing group (acyl group) onto the ring. Acetyl chloride (CH3COCl) gives acetophenone (C6H5COCH3).

C. Benzaldehyde: Benzaldehyde contains –CHO, whereas acetyl chloride introduces –COCH₃. Formyl chloride is unstable and is not a practical reagent for the standard Friedel-Crafts reaction, so benzene formylation uses a different method.

D. Benzoic acid: Benzoic acid contains –COOH, not the –COCH₃ group introduced here. The product is a ketone. In this acylation, the acylium electrophile resists rearrangement and the newly introduced carbonyl group discourages further ring acylation.

Key Educational Points:

  • Acetyl chloride introduces an acetyl group, –COCH₃, onto benzene.
  • The electrophile is a resonance-stabilized acylium ion.
  • The product's carbonyl group deactivates the ring, limiting further Friedel-Crafts acylation.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which class of alcohol commonly undergoes oxidation first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid without breaking its carbon skeleton?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Primary alcohol

Primary alcohols (RCH₂OH) can be oxidized first to an aldehyde (RCHO) and then further to a carboxylic acid (RCOOH) using strong oxidizing agents like KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇. Secondary alcohols ordinarily give ketones under standard alcohol-oxidation conditions; harsher oxidation can cleave carbon–carbon bonds. Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under normal conditions because they lack an H on the carbon bearing the -OH.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Tertiary alcohol: A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing –OH. It therefore resists the usual oxidation to a carbonyl compound without carbon–carbon bond cleavage.

B. Secondary alcohol: A secondary alcohol normally gives a ketone rather than an aldehyde. Converting that ketone further into smaller acids requires a different, more destructive oxidation pathway.

D. Phenol: Phenol has the -OH group bonded directly to an aromatic ring, which makes its oxidation chemistry completely different from aliphatic alcohols. Phenol does not undergo simple oxidation to a carboxylic acid like primary alcohols do. Instead, phenol can be oxidized to quinones under certain conditions, which is a fundamentally different pathway.

Key Educational Points:

  • A primary alcohol can give an aldehyde and, with further oxidation, a carboxylic acid.
  • A secondary alcohol normally gives a ketone under standard alcohol-oxidation conditions.
  • A tertiary alcohol lacks the required hydrogen on its –OH-bearing carbon and resists that usual pathway.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In the standard Lucas test, a small saturated tertiary alcohol that is initially soluble in the reagent typically produces cloudiness:
options: After several minutes at room temperature, with no immediate cloudiness
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Immediately at room temperature

Lucas reagent is concentrated HCl containing ZnCl₂. A suitable tertiary alcohol generally forms an insoluble alkyl chloride rapidly at room temperature, giving immediate cloudiness. The reaction is facilitated by formation of a relatively stable tertiary carbocation. Simple secondary alcohols are usually slower, while ordinary primary alcohols generally show no reaction during the room-temperature test. The timing is a practical guide, not an exact stopwatch rule; benzylic and allylic alcohols are important exceptions.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Only upon heating: Heating is not normally required for a suitable tertiary alcohol to give a positive Lucas test. Ordinary primary alcohols generally show no reaction during the room-temperature test. When they undergo substitution under suitable conditions, it usually proceeds by SN2, without a free primary carbocation.

B. After several minutes at room temperature, with no immediate cloudiness: Delayed cloudiness is more characteristic of a suitable secondary alcohol than a tertiary one. Exact timing varies with the alcohol and test conditions, so a fixed five-minute cutoff is not a universal rule.

D. Not at all: A suitable tertiary alcohol usually gives a rapid positive test because its conversion to an alkyl chloride is favorable under these conditions. The cloudy material is the poorly water-soluble chloride product.

Key Educational Points:

  • The Lucas test detects formation of a poorly water-soluble alkyl chloride as cloudiness.
  • Suitable tertiary alcohols usually react rapidly, secondary alcohols more slowly and ordinary primary alcohols poorly at room temperature.
  • Initial solubility and special structures such as benzylic or allylic alcohols can affect interpretation.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: When 2-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ under dehydration conditions, the major alkene product is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 2-methylbut-2-ene

According to Zaitsev's rule, the major product of elimination is the more substituted alkene. Dehydration of a tertiary alcohol proceeds via E1 mechanism through a stable tertiary carbocation. Removal of a proton from C3 gives the trisubstituted 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product over the less substituted 2-methylbut-1-ene.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 2-methylbut-1-ene: 2-methylbut-1-ene is the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product). According to Zaitsev's rule, the major product of E1 elimination (favored for tertiary alcohols with acid catalyst) is the more substituted alkene. 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted) is more stable than 2-methylbut-1-ene (disubstituted) and is therefore the major product.

C. 3-methylbut-1-ene: 3-Methylbut-1-ene places the double bond away from the carbon that originally bore –OH. It is not the direct β-elimination product of the initially formed tertiary carbocation. The major product comes from removing a β-hydrogen to form the more substituted 2-methylbut-2-ene.

D. Pent-1-ene: Pent-1-ene has an unbranched carbon skeleton. The normal dehydration of 2-methylbutan-2-ol retains its branch and mainly produces 2-methylbut-2-ene.

Key Educational Points:

  • Acid-catalyzed dehydration of this tertiary alcohol proceeds through a tertiary carbocation.
  • A β-hydrogen is removed to form a double bond adjacent to the carbocation carbon.
  • The more substituted alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, is the major product under these conditions.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which reagent is commonly used in anhydrous dichloromethane to convert a primary alcohol into an aldehyde while limiting further oxidation?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate)

PCC is used under anhydrous conditions to oxidize a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. In contrast, heating a primary alcohol with excess aqueous acidified dichromate or permanganate commonly gives a carboxylic acid. The conditions matter: an aldehyde can also be obtained with acidified dichromate by carefully controlling the oxidation and distilling the aldehyde away as it forms.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. KMnO₄ (acidic): Acidified permanganate commonly oxidizes a primary alcohol beyond the aldehyde stage under aqueous oxidation conditions. It is not the standard selective reagent in anhydrous dichloromethane described here.

B. K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺: Acidified dichromate can give an aldehyde if the product is removed by controlled distillation. With excess oxidant under aqueous reflux, further oxidation gives the carboxylic acid. PCC is the reagent associated with the anhydrous method in this stem.

D. Concentrated HNO₃: Concentrated HNO3 is a strong oxidizing acid, but it is not typically used for selective alcohol oxidation. It tends to cause harsh, non-selective oxidation and can nitrate aromatic rings. For controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde, mild, anhydrous reagents like PCC or Dess-Martin periodinane are preferred.

Key Educational Points:

  • PCC in anhydrous conditions commonly converts a primary alcohol into an aldehyde.
  • Excess aqueous oxidant and reflux can favor further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.
  • Removing an aldehyde by distillation can limit further oxidation even when dichromate is used.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Williamson ether synthesis involves the reaction of:
options: An alcohol with an alcohol using H₂SO₄
An alkoxide ion with a primary alkyl halide
A Grignard reagent with an epoxide
An alcohol with a carboxylic acid
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. An alkoxide ion with a primary alkyl halide

Williamson synthesis forms an ether when an alkoxide ion attacks a suitable alkyl halide by an SN2 reaction: RO⁻ + R′X → ROR′ + X⁻. Methyl and unhindered primary halides are especially useful. Secondary halides often give competing elimination, and tertiary halides are unsuitable for this SN2 route. The method can make both symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An alcohol with an alcohol using H₂SO₄: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of a suitable alcohol can form an ether, but that is a different method. For example, ethanol can give diethyl ether under controlled heating with sulfuric acid. The required conditions and competing alkene formation depend on the alcohol.

C. A Grignard reagent with an epoxide: A Grignard reagent opens an epoxide to form a magnesium alkoxide, which gives an alcohol after aqueous work-up. That carbon–carbon bond-forming reaction is different from an alkoxide forming an ether by SN2 substitution.

D. An alcohol with a carboxylic acid: An alcohol reacting with a carboxylic acid produces an ester (via Fischer esterification), not an ether. Esters have the general structure R-COO-R', while ethers have R-O-R'. The Williamson synthesis is an SN2 reaction, whereas esterification is a condensation/addition-elimination reaction.

Key Educational Points:

  • An alkoxide is the nucleophile in Williamson ether synthesis.
  • Methyl or unhindered primary alkyl halides favor the required SN2 reaction.
  • With a hindered halide, elimination can compete with or replace ether formation.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: When ethanol reacts with sodium metal, the products are:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Sodium ethoxide and H₂

Sodium reacts with ethanol to produce sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas: 2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂ONa + H₂. Sodium is oxidized to Na⁺, and hydrogen from the O–H groups is reduced to H₂. Ethanol often reacts less vigorously than water, but reaction speed alone does not establish relative acid strength.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Sodium ethanoate and H₂: Sodium ethanoate is the salt of ethanoic acid, not ethanol. Ethanoic acid with sodium metal can give sodium ethanoate and H₂; ethanol gives ethoxide because its carbon framework is not oxidized into a carboxyl group in this reaction.

C. Sodium ethoxide and H₂O: Sodium ethoxide and H2O is incorrect because the reaction produces H2 gas, not water. The sodium metal reduces the proton from the -OH group: 2 CH3CH2OH + 2 Na -> 2 CH3CH2ONa + H2 (gas). This is analogous to sodium reacting with water (2 Na + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2), but the reaction with ethanol is less vigorous.

D. Ethane and NaOH: Forming ethane would require removal of ethanol's oxygen-containing group. In this reaction the C–O bond remains intact: the O–H hydrogen is replaced by sodium to form ethoxide, and H₂ is released.

Key Educational Points:

  • Sodium metal reacts with ethanol to give sodium ethoxide and H₂.
  • Two alcohol molecules supply the two hydrogen atoms in one H₂ molecule.
  • Reaction rate and acid strength are different concepts; visible vigor alone does not measure acidity.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following gives a positive result with FeCl₃ solution (violet/green coloration)?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Phenol

Phenol gives a characteristic colored complex with Fe³⁺ under the usual ferric chloride test conditions, commonly a violet color for phenol itself. The exact color depends on the compound and conditions. The test is useful for phenols, but some enols and other suitable ligands also give positive reactions, so it is not absolutely specific for a phenolic aromatic ring.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ethanol: Ethanol does not give the characteristic positive phenol-test color under these conditions. Its ordinary aliphatic hydroxyl group behaves differently from the phenolic group in phenol. A positive ferric chloride test is not, however, restricted to aromatic compounds.

B. Diethyl ether: Diethyl ether does not give the characteristic phenol-test color. Its oxygen can donate a lone pair to a Lewis acid, so the absence of –OH does not mean that ethers are incapable of coordination; that is different from the colored reaction tested here.

D. Methanol: Methanol is an aliphatic alcohol and does not give the characteristic positive test under these conditions. Phenol does, but the test is not exclusive to phenols because some enols also form colored iron complexes.

Key Educational Points:

  • Phenol can form a colored coordination complex with Fe³⁺.
  • Ethanol, methanol and diethyl ether do not give the characteristic positive test here.
  • Some enols also test positive, so the result supports rather than uniquely proves a phenol identification.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In the usual aqueous comparison, which sequence lists these compounds from strongest to weakest acid?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Phenol > Water > Ethanol

The standard aqueous comparison is phenol > water > ethanol. Phenol is much more acidic because phenoxide is stabilized by resonance. Water and ethanol are much closer in acidity; the usual introductory comparison places water ahead of ethanol. Alkyl electron donation and solvation both affect the stability of ethoxide. Approximate aqueous pKₐ values of 10 for phenol and 16 for ethanol show the much larger separation between those two acids.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Water > Ethanol > Phenol: This sequence incorrectly places phenol last. Resonance stabilization of phenoxide makes phenol much more acidic than water or ethanol in the comparison used here.

C. Ethanol > Phenol > Water: This sequence incorrectly places ethanol first. Ethoxide lacks phenoxide's resonance stabilization, so ethanol is much less acidic than phenol and is placed below water in this aqueous comparison.

D. Ethanol > Water > Phenol: This sequence reverses the intended trend by putting ethanol first and phenol last. Compare conjugate-base stabilization and the stated aqueous conditions, rather than molecular mass.

Key Educational Points:

  • The standard aqueous order used here is phenol > water > ethanol.
  • Resonance stabilization makes phenoxide much more stable than a comparable localized alkoxide ion.
  • Acidity comparisons depend on the solvent; numerical pKₐ values must use compatible conventions.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Acid-catalyzed ring opening of an epoxide by water produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. A diol (1,2-diol)

An epoxide contains a strained three-membered ring with one oxygen atom. In acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, protonation makes the ring more susceptible to attack by water. One ring C–O bond breaks as a new bond forms between a ring carbon and the oxygen of water. Proton transfers give a 1,2-diol, with –OH groups on adjacent carbons.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. An aldehyde: The reaction specified is hydrolysis to a diol, not formation of an aldehyde. Some epoxides can rearrange to carbonyl compounds under other conditions without breaking a C–C bond, so oxidative cleavage is not a universal requirement.

C. A ketone: A ketone contains a C=O group flanked by two carbon groups. Epoxide ring-opening with water does not create a carbonyl group; instead, it adds two hydroxyl groups to give a diol. Ketones can be formed from epoxides through different reagents, such as rearrangement with Lewis acids under specific conditions.

D. An ether: Water opening an epoxide gives a diol. An alcohol nucleophile can instead give a hydroxy ether. In either case, nucleophilic attack forms a new C–O bond; the identity of the nucleophile determines the group introduced.

Key Educational Points:

  • Epoxides are strained three-membered cyclic ethers.
  • Acid-catalyzed attack by water opens the ring and gives adjacent hydroxyl groups.
  • One hydroxyl oxygen comes from the epoxide and the other from water.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is classified as:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. A trihydric alcohol

Glycerol (HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH) contains three hydroxyl groups, making it a trihydric alcohol (triol). It has two primary –OH groups and one secondary –OH group. Glycerol forms the backbone of triacylglycerols and glycerophospholipids.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A monohydric primary alcohol: A monohydric alcohol has only one -OH group (like ethanol). Glycerol has three -OH groups on three consecutive carbons, making it trihydric. "Primary" refers to the carbon type bearing the -OH, not the number of hydroxyl groups. Glycerol actually has two primary -OH groups (on C1 and C3) and one secondary -OH (on C2).

B. A dihydric secondary alcohol: A dihydric alcohol (diol) has two -OH groups, like ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol), which is used as antifreeze. Glycerol has three -OH groups, so it is trihydric. Additionally, calling it "secondary" is misleading since glycerol has both primary and secondary hydroxyl groups.

D. A phenol: A phenol has an -OH group directly bonded to a benzene ring. Glycerol is an aliphatic triol (propane-1,2,3-triol) with no aromatic ring. Phenols and alcohols differ significantly in acidity and chemical behavior because of the aromatic ring's electron effects on the -OH group.

Key Educational Points:

  • Glycerol contains three alcohol groups and is therefore a triol.
  • Its two terminal alcohol sites are primary and its middle alcohol site is secondary.
  • Glycerol is the backbone of triacylglycerols and glycerophospholipids, not all phospholipids.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which reagent is used in the Tollens' test to distinguish aldehydes from ketones?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Ammoniacal silver nitrate (Ag(NH₃)₂⁺)

Tollens' reagent contains the diamminesilver(I) ion, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, in an alkaline solution. An aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate while silver(I) is reduced to metallic silver, often forming a silver mirror. Ordinary simple ketones are negative, but some α-hydroxy ketones and reducing sugars can also give a positive result. The test is therefore not an absolute aldehyde-versus-every-ketone distinction.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Fehling's solution: Fehling's solution (Cu2+ in alkaline tartrate) also tests for aldehydes (forming a brick-red Cu2O precipitate) but is a different reagent from Tollens'. Fehling's test is better suited for aliphatic aldehydes and reducing sugars. It uses copper(II) ions rather than silver ions, and the positive result is a red precipitate rather than a silver mirror.

C. Benedict's solution: Benedict's solution is similar to Fehling's, containing Cu2+ ions in alkaline citrate solution. It also detects reducing sugars and aldehydes by producing a color change from blue to green, yellow, orange, or red (depending on concentration). However, Benedict's is not the reagent used in the Tollens' test.

D. Iodine in NaOH: Iodine in NaOH is used for the iodoform test, which gives a yellow CHI₃ precipitate with suitable methyl ketones. Ethanal, ethanol and alcohols of the form CH₃CH(OH)R also give the test under suitable conditions. This is different from the silver-deposition reaction of Tollens' reagent.

Key Educational Points:

  • Tollens' reagent contains [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ and can deposit metallic silver.
  • Aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylates under the alkaline test conditions.
  • Simple ketones are usually negative, but α-hydroxy ketones and reducing sugars prevent an absolute rule.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The reaction of a ketone with hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. An oxime

Hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) reacts with the carbonyl group of ketones (and aldehydes) through nucleophilic addition-elimination to form an oxime (C=N–OH). This is a condensation reaction with loss of water. Imines form with primary amines, hydrazones with hydrazine, and semicarbazones with semicarbazide.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An imine (Schiff base): An imine (Schiff base) is formed when a ketone or aldehyde reacts with a primary amine (R-NH2), not hydroxylamine. The product has a C=N-R linkage. Schiff bases are important intermediates in biological chemistry, such as in the mechanism of transaminase enzymes and in the visual cycle (retinal + opsin).

C. A hydrazone: A hydrazone is formed when a ketone or aldehyde reacts with hydrazine (NH2-NH2) or a substituted hydrazine. The product has a C=N-NH2 (or C=N-NHR) linkage. 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) reacts with carbonyl compounds to form orange/red 2,4-DNP hydrazones, which is a classic qualitative test.

D. A semicarbazone: A semicarbazone is formed when a ketone or aldehyde reacts with semicarbazide (NH2-NH-CO-NH2). These derivatives have sharp, characteristic melting points and were historically used to identify unknown carbonyl compounds before modern spectroscopy. Each nitrogen reagent (NH2OH, NH2NH2, semicarbazide) gives a different C=N derivative.

Key Educational Points:

  • Hydroxylamine reacts with an aldehyde or ketone to give an oxime, containing C=N–OH.
  • Formation of the oxime is a condensation reaction that releases water.
  • Different nitrogen reagents give different derivatives: hydroxylamine gives an oxime, hydrazine a hydrazone and semicarbazide a semicarbazone.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: What is the initial aldol addition product when two molecules of acetaldehyde (ethanal) react in cold dilute aqueous NaOH, before dehydration?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 3-hydroxybutanal

Base removes an α-hydrogen from one ethanal molecule to form an enolate. This attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule, forming a new C–C bond. Protonation gives CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO, 3-hydroxybutanal, a β-hydroxy aldehyde. This initial step is aldol addition. Subsequent loss of water gives but-2-enal; the addition followed by dehydration is commonly called aldol condensation.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Acetone: Acetone is a three-carbon ketone. The addition joins two two-carbon ethanal molecules to give a four-carbon β-hydroxy aldehyde, so acetone does not match the carbon count or functional groups.

C. Acetic acid: Ethanoic acid would result from oxidation of ethanal. The reaction here forms a new carbon–carbon bond between two ethanal molecules and gives a β-hydroxy aldehyde.

D. Crotonaldehyde (but-2-enal): But-2-enal is produced when 3-hydroxybutanal loses water. It is the later dehydration product, whereas the question asks for the initial addition product before dehydration.

Key Educational Points:

  • Aldol addition uses an enolate nucleophile to form a new C–C bond with a carbonyl compound.
  • Two ethanal molecules give the four-carbon β-hydroxy aldehyde 3-hydroxybutanal.
  • Dehydration gives but-2-enal; distinguish this later condensation product from the initial aldol addition product.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following carbonyl compounds does NOT undergo the iodoform reaction?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Benzaldehyde

Benzaldehyde lacks the CH₃CO– arrangement needed for this carbonyl comparison and gives a negative iodoform test. Acetone and butan-2-one are methyl ketones and are positive. Ethanal is also positive even though it is an aldehyde. Suitable alcohols can be positive after oxidation; ethanol is the important primary-alcohol example.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Acetaldehyde: Ethanal, CH₃CHO, gives a positive iodoform test. It is the usual aldehyde exception to the shorthand description of this as a methyl-ketone test.

B. Acetone: Acetone, CH₃COCH₃, is a methyl ketone. Under the test conditions it gives the characteristic yellow iodoform precipitate.

D. Methyl ethyl ketone: Methyl ethyl ketone is butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃. It contains a methyl group directly attached to the carbonyl carbon and therefore gives a positive iodoform test.

Key Educational Points:

  • Methyl ketones contain CH₃CO– and ordinarily give a positive iodoform test.
  • Ethanal and ethanol are important positive examples outside the methyl-ketone class.
  • Benzaldehyde lacks the required methyl-carbonyl arrangement and is negative.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The product of Grignard reaction between CH₃MgBr and formaldehyde (HCHO), after hydrolysis, is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Ethanol

The Grignard reagent CH₃MgBr adds to the carbonyl of formaldehyde (HCHO): CH₃MgBr + HCHO → CH₃CH₂OMgBr. Acidic hydrolysis gives ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH). Formaldehyde with a Grignard reagent always produces a primary alcohol.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Methanol: Methanol (CH3OH) has only one carbon and would result from reducing formaldehyde (HCHO) with NaBH4 or LiAlH4, not from a Grignard reaction. The Grignard reaction adds carbon atoms: CH3MgBr contributes one carbon to formaldehyde's one carbon, giving a two-carbon product (ethanol).

C. Propan-1-ol: Propan-1-ol can be prepared by adding ethylmagnesium bromide to formaldehyde, followed by aqueous work-up. The reagent in this question is methylmagnesium bromide, so the product has only two carbons and is ethanol.

D. Propan-2-ol: Propan-2-ol would result from CH₃MgBr adding to ethanal, followed by aqueous work-up. Adding CH₃MgBr to acetone instead gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The formaldehyde used here gives a primary alcohol.

Key Educational Points:

  • Grignard addition forms a C–C bond; aqueous work-up protonates the resulting alkoxide.
  • Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other ordinary aldehydes a secondary alcohol and ketones a tertiary alcohol.
  • CH₃MgBr supplies one carbon and formaldehyde supplies one carbon, giving two-carbon ethanol.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The classic Cannizzaro reaction in concentrated aqueous alkali is characteristic of aldehydes that:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Lack α-hydrogens

The Cannizzaro reaction occurs with aldehydes that have no α-hydrogens (such as formaldehyde and benzaldehyde) when treated with concentrated NaOH. One molecule is oxidized to a carboxylate and the other is reduced to an alcohol (disproportionation). Aldehydes with readily enolizable α-hydrogens generally favor competing aldol chemistry under basic conditions.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Have α-hydrogens: Aldehydes with readily enolizable alpha-hydrogens preferentially undergo the aldol reaction (not Cannizzaro) in base. The alpha-hydrogen is abstracted to form an enolate, which attacks another carbonyl. The Cannizzaro reaction specifically occurs with aldehydes that lack alpha-hydrogens (like formaldehyde, benzaldehyde, or trimethylacetaldehyde) because they cannot form enolates.

C. Are unsaturated: The presence of another double or triple bond is not the defining criterion. The classic examples are non-enolizable aldehydes such as benzaldehyde and formaldehyde, which lack α-hydrogens and can undergo disproportionation in concentrated alkali.

D. Contain a methyl group: Containing a methyl group is not relevant to the Cannizzaro reaction. In fact, acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) has a methyl group with alpha-hydrogens and undergoes aldol condensation, not the Cannizzaro reaction. The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation where one aldehyde molecule is oxidized to a carboxylate and another is reduced to an alcohol.

Key Educational Points:

  • Classic Cannizzaro substrates include formaldehyde and benzaldehyde, which have no α-hydrogens.
  • One aldehyde molecule is oxidized to a carboxylate while another is reduced to an alcohol.
  • Aldehydes with readily enolizable α-hydrogens commonly undergo competing aldol reactions in base.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Reduction of a ketone with NaBH₄ produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. A secondary alcohol

NaBH₄ is a mild reducing agent that selectively reduces the carbonyl group. A ketone (R₁COR₂) is reduced to a secondary alcohol (R₁CH(OH)R₂) because the carbon bearing the new –OH group remains bonded to two other carbon-containing groups. Most aldehydes give primary alcohols on reduction; formaldehyde gives methanol.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A primary alcohol: Reducing an aldehyde such as ethanal gives a primary alcohol. A ketone already has two carbon groups attached to its carbonyl carbon; those two groups remain attached after reduction, so the new alcohol site is secondary.

C. A tertiary alcohol: A tertiary alcohol has three carbon groups attached to the carbon bearing the -OH. Reducing a ketone (which has two carbon groups on the carbonyl carbon) with NaBH4 adds one hydrogen, giving a carbon with two carbon groups, one hydrogen, and one -OH. That is a secondary alcohol, not tertiary. Tertiary alcohols cannot be made by simple carbonyl reduction.

D. An alkane: An alkane would result from complete reduction that removes the oxygen entirely. NaBH4 is a mild reducing agent that reduces the C=O double bond to C-OH (adding H across the C=O bond) but does not remove the oxygen atom. Stronger conditions, like Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/HCl) or Wolff-Kishner reduction (NH2NH2/KOH), can fully reduce a carbonyl to a -CH2- group.

Key Educational Points:

  • NaBH₄ reduces a ketone's carbonyl group to an alcohol after protonation.
  • The alcohol-bearing carbon retains two carbon substituents, making the product secondary.
  • This reduction adds hydrogen without adding a carbon substituent or removing the oxygen atom.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following is the correct order of reactivity toward nucleophilic addition?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Formaldehyde > Acetaldehyde > Acetone

Reactivity toward nucleophilic addition decreases with increasing steric hindrance and increasing electron donation to the carbonyl carbon. Formaldehyde (HCHO) has the least steric hindrance and no electron-donating alkyl groups. Acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) has one methyl group, and acetone (CH₃COCH₃) has two, making it the least reactive.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Acetone > Formaldehyde > Acetaldehyde: Acetone > Formaldehyde > Acetaldehyde incorrectly places acetone first. Acetone is the least reactive toward nucleophilic addition because its two methyl groups create the most steric hindrance around the carbonyl carbon and donate the most electron density (reducing electrophilicity). Formaldehyde, with no alkyl groups, is the most reactive.

C. Acetaldehyde > Formaldehyde > Acetone: Acetaldehyde > Formaldehyde > Acetone incorrectly places acetaldehyde as most reactive. Formaldehyde (HCHO) has the highest reactivity because its carbonyl carbon has two small hydrogen atoms, offering minimal steric hindrance and no electron-donating alkyl groups. Reactivity decreases as more alkyl groups are attached: HCHO > CH3CHO > (CH3)2CO.

D. Acetone > Acetaldehyde > Formaldehyde: Acetone > Acetaldehyde > Formaldehyde is exactly backwards. Two factors determine nucleophilic addition reactivity: (1) steric effects, with more groups around the carbonyl making nucleophilic approach harder, and (2) electronic effects, with electron-donating alkyl groups reducing the partial positive charge on carbon. Both factors favor formaldehyde as most reactive.

Key Educational Points:

  • Formaldehyde is least hindered and has no electron-donating alkyl substituents on its carbonyl carbon.
  • Alkyl substituents both hinder nucleophilic approach and reduce carbonyl electrophilicity.
  • The usual comparison is formaldehyde > ethanal > acetone for nucleophilic addition.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The reaction of acetone with HCN produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Acetone cyanohydrin

HCN adds across the carbonyl of acetone via nucleophilic addition. The CN− ion attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, and subsequent protonation gives the cyanohydrin: (CH₃)₂C(OH)(CN). Cyanohydrin formation is a key reaction for extending the carbon chain and introducing functional groups.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Acetonitrile: Acetonitrile (CH3CN) is a nitrile formed by dehydration of acetamide or by reaction of methyl halide with cyanide, not by HCN addition to a ketone. The cyanohydrin reaction is a nucleophilic addition where CN- attacks the carbonyl carbon and H+ protonates the oxygen, giving (CH3)2C(OH)(CN), which is acetone cyanohydrin.

C. Lactic acid: Hydrolysis of acetone cyanohydrin's nitrile group gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂C(OH)COOH, after acidic work-up. It does not give lactic acid. Lactic acid has three carbons and can instead be obtained by hydrolyzing the cyanohydrin of ethanal. The immediate product asked for here is acetone cyanohydrin.

D. Acrylonitrile: Acrylonitrile (CH2=CHCN) is an unsaturated nitrile used in polymer production (polyacrylonitrile). It is made industrially by ammoxidation of propene, not by adding HCN to acetone. The HCN addition to a carbonyl is a nucleophilic addition reaction, preserving the carbon-oxygen bond as a hydroxyl group.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon, and protonation gives a cyanohydrin.
  • The original carbonyl carbon ends up bonded to both –OH and –CN.
  • Cyanohydrin formation adds one carbon; acetone's three carbons become four in its cyanohydrin.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: An aldehyde is treated with excess alcohol and an acid catalyst while water is removed. Which product is favored?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. An acetal

An alcohol first adds to the aldehyde to form a hemiacetal, with –OH and –OR on the same carbon. Further reaction with alcohol under acid catalysis can give an acetal, with two –OR groups on that carbon, plus water. The reaction is reversible: excess alcohol and removal of water favor acetal formation, whereas aqueous acid favors hydrolysis. Some cyclic hemiacetals, including those in sugars, are stable and abundant.

Why the other choices are wrong:
