A. A hemiacetal: A hemiacetal has one –OH and one –OR group on the former carbonyl carbon. Under the stated conditions, further reaction and removal of water favor the acetal. Hemiacetals are not universally unstable; cyclic sugar forms are important examples.

C. An ester: An ester (R-COOR') is formed by the reaction of a carboxylic acid (not an aldehyde) with an alcohol under acid catalysis (Fischer esterification). The aldehyde carbonyl carbon is at a lower oxidation state than a carboxylic acid, so the product of aldehyde + alcohol is an acetal, not an ester.

D. An enol ether: An enol ether has an alkoxy group attached to a C=C bond. The favored product here instead has two –OR groups on the former aldehyde carbon and no carbonyl-derived C=C bond.

Key Educational Points:

  • A hemiacetal has –OH and –OR on one carbon; an acetal has two –OR groups there.
  • Excess alcohol and removal of water favor acetal formation in this reversible reaction.
  • Acetals can protect carbonyl groups and can be hydrolyzed with aqueous acid.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following carboxylic acids is the strongest?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Cl₃CCOOH

Electron-withdrawing groups (like Cl) stabilize the carboxylate conjugate base through the inductive effect (-I). More chlorine atoms increase the electron-withdrawing power, stabilizing the negative charge more effectively. Thus acidity increases: CH₃COOH < ClCH₂COOH < Cl₂CHCOOH < Cl₃CCOOH (trichloroacetic acid, pKₐ ≈ 0.65).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. CH₃COOH: Acetic acid (CH3COOH, pKa 4.76) is the weakest acid in this series because the methyl group is slightly electron-donating, which destabilizes the carboxylate anion. With no electron-withdrawing substituents, acetic acid serves as the baseline for comparing substituent effects on acidity.

B. ClCH₂COOH: Chloroacetic acid (ClCH2COOH, pKa 2.86) is stronger than acetic acid because the chlorine atom withdraws electron density through the inductive effect, stabilizing the carboxylate anion. However, it has only one chlorine, so its inductive effect is weaker than that of dichloro- or trichloroacetic acid.

C. Cl₂CHCOOH: Dichloroacetic acid (Cl2CHCOOH, pKa 1.29) is stronger than monochloroacetic acid because two chlorine atoms exert a greater electron-withdrawing inductive effect. However, trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH, pKa 0.65) is even stronger because three chlorines provide the maximum inductive withdrawal in this series.

Key Educational Points:

  • Chlorine substituents withdraw electron density through the inductive effect.
  • Stabilizing the carboxylate conjugate base increases the acid's strength.
  • In this series, acidity increases from acetic acid to mono-, di- and trichloroacetic acid.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Fischer esterification involves the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in the presence of:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. An acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄)

Fischer esterification is an acid-catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to form an ester and water: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O. The acid catalyst protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic. The reaction is reversible, so excess alcohol or removal of water shifts the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A base catalyst: A base mainly deprotonates the starting carboxylic acid to form a carboxylate salt, rather than catalyzing Fischer esterification. This reaction uses acid to make the carbonyl more susceptible to attack by the alcohol.

C. NaOH: NaOH is a strong base that would deprotonate the carboxylic acid to form a carboxylate salt (RCOO- Na+), which is unreactive toward nucleophilic attack by an alcohol. In fact, NaOH is the reagent used for ester hydrolysis (saponification), which is the opposite of esterification.

D. LiAlH₄: LiAlH₄ is a reducing reagent, not a Fischer esterification catalyst. With sufficient reagent under suitable anhydrous conditions, a carboxylic acid can be reduced to a primary alcohol after aqueous work-up. The acidic proton consumes some hydride, but it does not make carboxylic-acid reduction impossible. Reducing one carboxylic-acid molecule does not generate the two alcohol molecules obtained by reducing an ester.

Key Educational Points:

  • Fischer esterification combines a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to give an ester and water.
  • Acid catalysis increases the carbonyl's susceptibility to nucleophilic attack.
  • Removing water or using excess alcohol shifts the equilibrium toward the ester.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The correct order of reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Acid chloride > Anhydride > Ester > Amide

Reactivity depends on the leaving group ability and the electron donation to the carbonyl. Acid chlorides are most reactive (Cl− is a good leaving group, minimal resonance stabilization). Amides are least reactive because the nitrogen lone pair strongly stabilizes the carbonyl through resonance, and NH₂⁻ is a poor leaving group.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ester > Amide > Acid chloride > Anhydride: This order incorrectly places esters and amides above acid chlorides and anhydrides. The usual relative leaving-group ability is Cl⁻ > RCOO⁻ > RO⁻ > NH₂⁻. Chloride and carboxylate leave more readily; alkoxide and especially amide anions are poor leaving groups. Resonance donation into the acyl group also affects reactivity.

C. Amide > Ester > Anhydride > Acid chloride: Amide > Ester > Anhydride > Acid chloride is also backwards. Amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives because nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl by resonance, stabilizing the amide group and making it resistant to nucleophilic attack. This is why peptide bonds (amide bonds) are kinetically stable in proteins.

D. Anhydride > Acid chloride > Amide > Ester: Anhydride > Acid chloride > Amide > Ester incorrectly places anhydrides above acid chlorides. Acid chlorides are the most reactive because Cl- is the best leaving group (weakest base) among the four. The full reactivity order is: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, corresponding to decreasing leaving group ability.

Key Educational Points:

  • The usual order is acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.
  • Better leaving groups generally make nucleophilic acyl substitution easier.
  • Nitrogen-to-carbonyl resonance donation makes ordinary amides especially resistant to this reaction.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) with NaOH is called:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Saponification

Saponification is the base-promoted hydrolysis of an ester. Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl, ultimately giving a carboxylate salt and an alcohol: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + CH₃CH₂OH. Hydroxide is consumed in the overall reaction. Formation of the carboxylate makes the process strongly product-favored under these alkaline conditions; acidification in a separate step would give the carboxylic acid.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Esterification: Esterification is the formation of an ester from an acid and alcohol, which is the reverse of what this question describes. The question describes ester hydrolysis (breaking the ester bond), not ester formation. Fischer esterification (acid-catalyzed) makes esters; saponification (base-promoted hydrolysis) breaks them.

C. Transesterification: Transesterification replaces an ester's alkoxy group with that from another alcohol, producing a different ester and an alcohol. Saponification instead converts the ester to a carboxylate salt. Some transesterification methods are base-catalyzed, so the presence of a base alone does not identify the reaction.

D. Decarboxylation: Decarboxylation is the loss of CO2 from a carboxylic acid or its derivative. It has nothing to do with ester hydrolysis. An example of decarboxylation is heating a beta-keto acid, which loses CO2 to give a ketone. Saponification, by contrast, breaks the ester into a carboxylate salt and an alcohol.

Key Educational Points:

  • Ester hydrolysis with hydroxide gives a carboxylate and an alcohol.
  • Hydroxide is consumed overall, so this is base-promoted rather than simply base-catalyzed hydrolysis.
  • Acidifying the carboxylate afterward gives the corresponding carboxylic acid.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Decarboxylation of sodium acetate with soda lime (NaOH/CaO) produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Methane

Heating sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) causes decarboxylation: CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃. The product alkane has one fewer carbon than the original acid. This is a classic method for preparing methane in the laboratory.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ethane: Ethane has two carbon atoms. Here, the carboxyl carbon of two-carbon sodium acetate ends up in carbonate, leaving a one-carbon hydrocarbon product, methane. The balanced equation accounts for both original carbon atoms.

C. Ethene: Ethene has two carbons and a C=C bond. Sodium acetate instead gives one-carbon methane in this reaction. The stated reaction replaces the carboxylate group with hydrogen; it does not create an alkene from this substrate.

D. Acetone: Acetone ((CH3)2CO) has three carbons and a carbonyl group. The decarboxylation of sodium acetate removes the carboxyl carbon into Na2CO3, producing the simplest alkane, methane. Acetone can be formed by dry distillation of calcium acetate, which is a different reaction entirely.

Key Educational Points:

  • Heating sodium acetate with soda lime gives methane and sodium carbonate.
  • The hydrocarbon product has one carbon fewer than the starting acetate ion.
  • The removed carboxyl carbon remains accounted for in carbonate.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following is an anhydride?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. (CH₃CO)₂O

Acetic anhydride (CH₃CO)₂O has the general structure of two acyl groups bonded to the same oxygen (RCO–O–COR). CH₃COOCH₃ is an ester (methyl acetate), CH₃CONHCH₃ is an amide (N-methylacetamide), and CH₃COCl is an acid chloride (acetyl chloride).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. CH₃COOCH₃: CH3COOCH3 is methyl acetate, an ester (not an anhydride). Carboxylic esters contain R–C(=O)–O–R′, where R′ can be an alkyl group, as here, or an aryl group. An anhydride, by contrast, has two acyl groups linked by an oxygen: R-CO-O-CO-R', which can be thought of as two carboxylic acid molecules minus one water.

B. CH₃CONHCH₃: CH₃CONHCH₃ is N-methylacetamide, containing a carbonyl carbon bonded to nitrogen. Its N–H group can donate hydrogen bonds, while its carbonyl oxygen can accept them. Its resistance to hydrolysis is mainly explained by amide resonance and poor leaving-group ability, not by the mere presence of an N–H bond.

D. CH₃COCl: CH3COCl is acetyl chloride, an acid chloride (acyl chloride). Acid chlorides have the structure R-CO-Cl and are the most reactive carboxylic acid derivatives. They react vigorously with water, alcohols, and amines. The four common carboxylic acid derivatives are: acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters, and amides.

Key Educational Points:

  • An acid anhydride has two acyl groups connected through an oxygen atom.
  • Acetic anhydride is CH₃CO–O–COCH₃, often written (CH₃CO)₂O.
  • Distinguish anhydrides from esters, amides and acid chlorides by the group attached to the acyl carbon.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Aspirin is produced by the acetylation of salicylic acid with:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Acetic anhydride

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is synthesized by treating salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) with acetic anhydride. The phenolic –OH group is acetylated to form an ester linkage. Acetic anhydride is preferred over acetic acid because the reaction is faster and more complete.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Acetic acid: Acetic acid is much less effective than acetic anhydride for acetylating salicylic acid's phenolic hydroxyl group in the standard laboratory synthesis. Acetic anhydride provides an activated acetyl group and is the intended reagent here.

C. Acetaldehyde: Acetaldehyde does not transfer an acetyl group in the reaction used to make aspirin. Forming aspirin requires an ester at the phenolic oxygen, which is readily achieved with an activated acetyl donor such as acetic anhydride.

D. Acetone: Acetone (CH3COCH3) is a ketone that does not serve as an acetylating agent. Ketones are relatively unreactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution because they lack a good leaving group. To make aspirin, you need acetic anhydride (or acetyl chloride), which can donate an acetyl group to the phenolic -OH of salicylic acid.

Key Educational Points:

  • Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid.
  • Acetylation converts salicylic acid's phenolic hydroxyl group into an ester.
  • Acetic anhydride supplies the acetyl group; the carboxylic-acid group is retained.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following compounds has the highest normal boiling point at 1 atm?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Butanamide (MW 87)

Butanamide has the highest normal boiling point in this set, about 216 °C. Its primary amide group has N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl oxygen that accepts hydrogen bonds, allowing strong intermolecular association. Its large amide dipole also contributes. The result depends on the combined intermolecular interactions and molecular structure, not molecular mass alone or a universal claim that N–H hydrogen bonds exceed O–H hydrogen bonds in strength.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Ethyl acetate (MW 88): Ethyl acetate boils at about 77 °C. Its oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, but it has no O–H or N–H group to donate hydrogen bonds between its own molecules, so it lacks butanamide's extensive self-association.

B. Propionic acid (MW 74): Propionic acid boils at about 141 °C and associates strongly through hydrogen bonding. It nevertheless boils below butanamide in this set. Compare the overall interactions of these compounds rather than assuming that every amide–amide hydrogen bond is stronger than every acid–acid hydrogen bond.

D. Butanoyl chloride (MW 107): Butanoyl chloride boils at about 102 °C despite its higher molecular mass. It is polar and can participate in interactions with hydrogen-bond donors, but it has no O–H or N–H group for the strong self-association available to butanamide.

Key Educational Points:

  • Boiling points reflect intermolecular attraction as well as molecular size and shape.
  • In a primary amide, N–H groups donate hydrogen bonds and the carbonyl oxygen accepts them.
  • Butanamide boils highest in this set; molecular mass alone does not predict the ranking.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: In Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky bromination of butanoic acid, followed by aqueous work-up, which carbon has a hydrogen replaced by bromine in the final acid product?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The α-carbon

The HVZ reaction uses Br₂ with a catalytic amount of PBr₃ (or red phosphorus) to selectively brominate the α-carbon of a carboxylic acid. The mechanism involves formation of an acid bromide, which enolizes more readily than the acid itself, followed by α-bromination. The substrate must have an α-hydrogen. Aqueous work-up converts the acyl bromide back into a carboxylic acid, so the product is an α-bromo carboxylic acid; butanoic acid gives 2-bromobutanoic acid.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The carbonyl carbon: An acyl bromide is an intermediate, so bromine is temporarily bonded to the carbonyl carbon. Aqueous work-up restores the carboxylic-acid group. The hydrogen-to-bromine substitution retained in the final product is on the adjacent α-carbon.

C. The β-carbon: The β-carbon (two carbons away from the carbonyl) is not the site of bromination in the HVZ reaction. Alpha-bromination is favored because the enol intermediate places a reactive double bond between the α-carbon and the carbonyl carbon, making the alpha position the site of electrophilic attack by bromine.

D. The terminal carbon: In butanoic acid, the terminal methyl carbon is C4, whereas the α-carbon is C2. The reaction brominates C2 through an enol intermediate, not the terminal C4 position.

Key Educational Points:

  • HVZ bromination replaces an α-hydrogen in a suitable carboxylic acid.
  • An acyl bromide and its enol participate before aqueous work-up restores the acid group.
  • Butanoic acid gives 2-bromobutanoic acid, distinguishing its α-carbon from its terminal carbon.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: After treatment of an alkyl carboxylic acid (RCOOH) with excess LiAlH₄ followed by aqueous work-up, the organic product is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. A primary alcohol

LiAlH₄ reduces RCOOH to RCH₂OH after aqueous work-up, giving a primary alcohol. Sufficient reagent is needed because the acidic proton also consumes hydride. Reduction proceeds beyond the aldehyde oxidation level, so an aldehyde is not normally isolated. Ordinary NaBH₄ alone does not perform this carboxylic-acid reduction under standard conditions.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An aldehyde: An aldehyde is not normally isolated because the reducing conditions also convert that carbonyl functionality to an alcohol. The product after work-up is RCH₂OH.

C. A secondary alcohol: A secondary alcohol has two carbon substituents on the carbon bearing the -OH. Reducing a carboxylic acid (R-COOH) gives R-CH2OH, which is a primary alcohol (only one carbon substituent on the -OH-bearing carbon). Secondary alcohols are formed by reducing ketones, not carboxylic acids.

D. An alkane: An alkane would have lost the oxygen functionality entirely. This carboxylic-acid reduction retains one oxygen as the alcohol group, producing RCH₂OH rather than removing that oxygen to give an alkane.

Key Educational Points:

  • Excess LiAlH₄ followed by aqueous work-up converts an alkyl carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.
  • The carboxyl carbon is retained as the alcohol-bearing carbon.
  • Standard NaBH₄ conditions reduce aldehydes and ketones but not ordinary carboxylic acids.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which sequence gives the correct order of base strength in dilute aqueous solution near 25 °C?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > NH₃

In this aqueous comparison, dimethylamine is slightly more basic than methylamine, and both are more basic than ammonia. Alkyl electron donation favors proton acceptance, but water stabilizes the bases and their conjugate acids differently. The observed order therefore depends on both electronic effects and solvation, not simply on counting methyl groups.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. NH₃ > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₂NH: This sequence puts ammonia ahead of the two methyl-substituted amines. In water, methylamine and dimethylamine are stronger bases than ammonia, so that ranking is reversed.

C. CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₂NH > NH₃: Methylamine and dimethylamine are close in aqueous basicity, but dimethylamine is slightly stronger under the stated conditions. Adding an alkyl group does not provide a universal ranking for every amine in every solvent.

D. (CH₃)₃N > (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂: Trimethylamine is less basic than dimethylamine in water; the ordering shown is associated with the gas-phase comparison instead. Trimethylammonium, (CH₃)₃NH⁺, has one N–H bond and can donate a hydrogen bond. Its solvation is less favorable than that of the less substituted ammonium ions; it does not lack N–H bonds altogether.

Key Educational Points:

  • The aqueous order in this comparison is (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > NH₃.
  • Both electron donation and solvation affect amine basicity.
  • Protonating trimethylamine gives (CH₃)₃NH⁺, which has one N–H bond; gas-phase and aqueous rankings can differ.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Aniline is a weaker base than cyclohexylamine because:
options: Aniline has a higher molecular weight
The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalized into the benzene ring
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalized into the benzene ring

In aniline, the nitrogen lone pair participates in resonance with the aromatic π system, reducing its availability for protonation. In cyclohexylamine, no such delocalization occurs (the ring is saturated), so the nitrogen lone pair is fully available as a base. This makes cyclohexylamine significantly more basic than aniline.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Aniline has a higher molecular weight: Aniline, C₆H₇N, actually has a lower molecular mass than cyclohexylamine, C₆H₁₃N. Molecular mass does not explain the basicity difference. The key structural distinction here is delocalization of aniline's nitrogen lone pair into the aromatic ring.

C. Aniline has more hydrogen atoms: Aniline actually has fewer hydrogen atoms than cyclohexylamine, but this is irrelevant to basicity. The number of hydrogens on a molecule does not determine how readily the nitrogen lone pair accepts a proton. The key factor is lone pair delocalization: in cyclohexylamine, the lone pair is fully localized on nitrogen and readily available for protonation.

D. Cyclohexylamine has a phenyl group: This statement has the structures confused. Cyclohexylamine has a cyclohexyl group (saturated ring), not a phenyl group (aromatic ring). Aniline is the one with the phenyl group. The aromatic ring in aniline is what reduces basicity by delocalizing the nitrogen lone pair through resonance, which cannot happen with the saturated cyclohexane ring.

Key Educational Points:

  • Aniline's nitrogen lone pair can delocalize into its aromatic ring.
  • This reduces its availability for protonation compared with an ordinary alkylamine.
  • Cyclohexylamine has a saturated ring and lacks this aromatic lone-pair delocalization.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which amino acid has a nonpolar, hydrophobic side chain?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Leucine

Leucine has an isobutyl side chain (–CH₂CH(CH₃)₂), which is entirely hydrocarbon and therefore nonpolar and hydrophobic. Serine has a polar hydroxyl group; at physiological pH the side chain of aspartate contains –COO⁻ and that of lysine is predominantly –NH₃⁺.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Serine: Serine's side chain is –CH₂OH. Its hydroxyl group can form hydrogen bonds, making the side chain polar rather than hydrocarbon-like and hydrophobic.

B. Aspartate: Aspartate's side chain is predominantly –CH₂COO⁻ at physiological pH. This negative charge interacts strongly with water, unlike leucine's nonpolar side chain.

D. Lysine: Lysine's side-chain amino group is predominantly protonated as –NH₃⁺ at physiological pH. That positive charge makes the side chain hydrophilic rather than nonpolar.

Key Educational Points:

  • Leucine's side chain is a nonpolar hydrocarbon group.
  • Serine is polar, while aspartate and lysine have charged side chains near physiological pH.
  • Classify side chains separately from the amino acid's shared backbone groups.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: At its isoelectric point in aqueous solution, free glycine exists predominantly as:
options: A molecule with no charged functional groups
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. A zwitterion

Near its isoelectric point, about pH 6, free glycine is predominantly ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, a zwitterion. It contains both a positive and a negative charge but has zero net charge in this form. At the isoelectric point the population has zero average net charge and no net electrophoretic migration. Zero net charge does not mean that all functional groups are uncharged.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A cation: At sufficiently low pH, glycine is mainly ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH and has net charge +1. Near its isoelectric point, loss of the carboxyl proton makes the zwitterion predominant instead.

B. An anion: At sufficiently high pH, glycine is mainly H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻ and has net charge −1. That is above its isoelectric point, not the predominant form at the pI.

D. A molecule with no charged functional groups: The structure H₂N–CH₂–COOH has no charged functional groups, but it is not glycine's predominant form at its pI in water. The predominant zwitterion has charged groups whose contributions cancel.

Key Educational Points:

  • A zwitterion contains both positive and negative charges within the same molecular species.
  • Free glycine is predominantly ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻ near its pI, about pH 6.
  • The isoelectric point concerns zero average net charge, not absence of all charged groups.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The peptide bond between two amino acids is:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. An amide bond

A peptide bond is an amide linkage between the carboxyl-derived carbonyl carbon of one amino-acid residue and the amino nitrogen of the next. Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, making the peptide unit approximately planar and restricting rotation. The linkage is often written –CO–NH–, but a peptide bond to proline's nitrogen has no N–H hydrogen.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An ester bond: A carboxylic ester connects an acyl group to an oxygen-containing group, as in the fatty-acid esters of glycerol. A peptide instead contains an acyl carbon–nitrogen linkage. DNA and RNA have phosphodiester links, which are esters of phosphate and are structurally different from carboxylic esters.

B. A glycosidic bond: Glycosidic bonds involve a sugar's anomeric carbon. The common O-glycosidic links between sugars differ from the carbonyl carbon–nitrogen amide linkage in a peptide bond.

D. A disulfide bond: A disulfide bond joins two cysteine side chains through an S–S linkage and can stabilize protein structure. It does not replace the peptide bonds connecting successive residues. The backbone also contains the other covalent bonds within each amino-acid residue.

Key Educational Points:

  • Peptide bonds are amide linkages connecting amino-acid residues.
  • Resonance makes the peptide unit approximately planar and restricts rotation about its C–N bond.
  • Disulfide bonds connect cysteine side chains, whereas peptide bonds connect residues along the backbone.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Treatment of a primary aromatic amine with nitrous acid in hydrochloric acid at 0–5 °C gives a relatively persistent intermediate. Which type of compound is it?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. A diazonium salt

Primary aromatic amines react with HNO₂ (generated from NaNO₂ + HCl) at 0–5°C to form relatively stable diazonium salts (ArN₂⁺Cl−). These are important intermediates in organic synthesis for Sandmeyer reactions and azo dye formation. Primary aliphatic amines also form diazonium salts, but they decompose rapidly to give nitrogen gas and carbocations.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A secondary amine: A secondary amine would require a second carbon-containing group on nitrogen. Nitrous acid does not simply alkylate the starting amine; under the stated conditions it converts the primary aromatic amino group into an arenediazonium group.

C. A nitrile: A nitrile (R-CN) is formed by dehydrating primary amides or by nucleophilic substitution with cyanide. It is not a product of primary amine + HNO2. The diazonium salt formed in this reaction is a versatile synthetic intermediate that can be converted to phenols, halides, nitriles (via Sandmeyer reaction), and azo dyes.

D. An amide: Forming an amide from this amine would require an acylating reagent, such as an acid chloride or anhydride. Nitrous acid performs diazotization instead. Acylating a primary amine normally gives an N-substituted amide, not necessarily RCONH₂.

Key Educational Points:

  • Primary aromatic amines form arenediazonium ions with nitrous acid in cold acidic solution.
  • Low temperature helps preserve the intermediate for subsequent reactions.
  • Aliphatic diazonium ions are much less persistent and commonly lose N₂ rapidly.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Gabriel synthesis is used to prepare:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Primary amines

The Gabriel synthesis uses potassium phthalimide, which acts as a nucleophile in an SN2 reaction with a primary alkyl halide. Subsequent hydrolysis (or treatment with hydrazine - Ing-Manske procedure) releases the primary amine. This method avoids over-alkylation problems because the nitrogen in phthalimide is only monoalkylated.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Secondary amines: Gabriel synthesis cannot produce secondary amines because the phthalimide nitrogen can only be alkylated once before hydrolysis. The method involves potassium phthalimide reacting with a primary alkyl halide (SN2), then hydrolysis releases the primary amine. For secondary amines, other methods like reductive amination are used.

B. Tertiary amines: Tertiary amines cannot be made by Gabriel synthesis for the same reason. The phthalimide nitrogen is already bonded to two carbonyl carbons, so only one alkyl group can be introduced. Gabriel synthesis is valued precisely because it avoids the over-alkylation problem that plagues direct amine synthesis.

D. Quaternary ammonium salts: Quaternary ammonium salts contain R₄N⁺ ions, with four carbon-containing groups bonded to nitrogen; these can be alkyl or aryl groups. Gabriel synthesis instead releases a primary amine, RNH₂. A quaternary ammonium salt can be prepared by alkylating a tertiary amine.

Key Educational Points:

  • Phthalimide anion substitutes on a suitable primary alkyl halide by SN2.
  • Cleavage of the resulting N-alkyl phthalimide releases a primary amine.
  • The method avoids repeated alkylation of a free amine during the substitution step.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which of the following amino acids contains sulfur?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cysteine

Cysteine contains a thiol group, –SH, in its side chain. Oxidation can join two cysteine sulfur atoms in a disulfide bond; the disulfide-linked pair is called cystine. Such links can stabilize protein structure. Methionine also contains sulfur, but in a thioether group rather than a free thiol.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Valine: Valine is a branched-chain, nonpolar amino acid with the side chain -CH(CH3)2. It contains only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, with no sulfur. Valine is one of the three branched-chain amino acids (along with leucine and isoleucine) that are essential in human nutrition.

C. Tyrosine: Tyrosine's side chain is –CH₂–C₆H₄–OH, with –OH opposite the –CH₂– attachment on the benzene ring. It contains no sulfur. Tyrosine is important as a precursor to several key biomolecules: dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroid hormones, and melanin.

D. Histidine: Histidine contains an imidazole ring with nitrogen atoms and no sulfur. Among the standard twenty amino acids, cysteine has a thiol and methionine has a thioether. Methionine's side chain does not ordinarily form the disulfide links characteristic of cysteine.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cysteine has a sulfur-containing thiol side chain.
  • Two cysteines can be oxidized to a disulfide-linked pair, cystine.
  • Methionine's sulfur is in a thioether, which behaves differently from cysteine's thiol.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: When a suitable quaternary ammonium hydroxide is heated and more than one alkene position is possible, the usual Hofmann-elimination preference is for:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The least substituted alkene (Hofmann product)

Hofmann elimination removes a β-hydrogen and a tertiary amine leaving group from a quaternary ammonium ion, forming an alkene on heating. The less substituted alkene is often favored because removal of a less hindered β-hydrogen is easier. The usual exhaustive-methylation route releases trimethylamine, but a general quaternary ammonium salt can release a different tertiary amine. Substrate structure and the required elimination geometry can affect the outcome.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The most substituted alkene (Zaitsev product): The more substituted alkene is the usual Zaitsev product. Hofmann elimination often favors the less substituted alternative because of the accessibility of the β-hydrogen, although this is a trend rather than an exceptionless rule.

C. An alcohol: The elimination produces an alkene, a tertiary amine and water. Hydroxide removes a β-hydrogen rather than replacing the ammonium group with –OH in the reaction described here.

D. An amine oxide: An amine oxide is produced by a different reaction: oxidation of a tertiary amine with a peroxide (like H2O2 or mCPBA). Amine oxide elimination (Cope elimination) is a related but distinct reaction. Hofmann elimination specifically involves heating a quaternary ammonium hydroxide, often favoring the less substituted alkene.

Key Educational Points:

  • Heating a suitable quaternary ammonium hydroxide can give an alkene, a tertiary amine and water.
  • Hofmann elimination often favors the less substituted alkene.
  • A β-hydrogen and suitable elimination geometry are required; the preference is not universal.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The Hinsberg test distinguishes between primary, secondary, and tertiary amines using:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Benzenesulfonyl chloride (C₆H₅SO₂Cl)

The Hinsberg test uses benzenesulfonyl chloride in alkaline solution. A primary amine forms a sulfonamide with an N–H proton; deprotonation gives a salt that is soluble in alkali in the standard test. A secondary amine forms a sulfonamide with no N–H proton, so it does not show this base-solubilization behavior. A tertiary amine does not form the diagnostic sulfonamide. The unchanged tertiary amine can be protonated by dilute acid.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. FeCl₃ solution: FeCl3 solution is used to test for phenols (giving a characteristic violet, green, or blue color due to complex formation with Fe3+ ions) and for enols. It does not distinguish between amine classes. The Hinsberg test specifically uses benzenesulfonyl chloride, which reacts differently with primary, secondary, and tertiary amines.

C. Tollens' reagent: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO3) is used to detect aldehydes by oxidizing them to carboxylates while reducing Ag+ to metallic silver (the "silver mirror" test). It has no application in amine classification. The Hinsberg comparison instead depends on sulfonamide formation and whether the product can be deprotonated in alkali.

D. Ninhydrin solution: Ninhydrin solution is used to detect alpha-amino acids and primary amines, producing a characteristic purple color (Ruhemann's purple). While ninhydrin does react with amines, it does not distinguish between primary, secondary, and tertiary amines the way the Hinsberg test does.

Key Educational Points:

  • Benzenesulfonyl chloride is the reagent in the Hinsberg test.
  • A primary-amine sulfonamide retains an N–H proton that allows formation of an alkali-soluble salt.
  • Secondary-amine sulfonamides lack that proton; tertiary amines do not form the diagnostic sulfonamide.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: How many structural isomers does C₄H₁₀ have?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 2

C₄H₁₀ (butane) has two structural isomers: n-butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) with a straight chain, and isobutane or 2-methylpropane (CH(CH₃)₃) with a branched chain. These differ in the connectivity of their carbon atoms.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 1: One isomer would mean C4H10 has only one possible structure, but there are two: n-butane (a straight chain of four carbons, CH3CH2CH2CH3) and isobutane (2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CH, with a branched structure). Even with just four carbons, branching creates a second structural isomer.

C. 3: Three structural isomers is incorrect for C4H10. There are only two ways to arrange four carbon atoms: as a straight chain (butane) or with one branch (2-methylpropane). The number of structural isomers grows rapidly with carbon count: C5H12 has 3, C6H14 has 5, C7H16 has 9, and C10H22 has 75.

D. 4: Four structural isomers is too many for C4H10. With only four carbons, the branching options are very limited. You can have a straight chain or a single methyl branch (there is only one position for it). Compare this to C5H12, which has 3 isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane, and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).

Key Educational Points:

  • Structural (constitutional) isomers share a molecular formula but differ in how the atoms are connected.
  • C₄H₁₀ has exactly two: n-butane, a straight chain, and methylpropane (isobutane), which is branched.
  • Count systematically - shorten the main chain by one and move the branch - and check that each new structure is genuinely different, not the same skeleton drawn at another angle.
  • Branching lowers the boiling point, because a more compact molecule presents less surface for London dispersion forces.
  • Structural isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers have identical connectivity and differ only in spatial arrangement.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: For an alkene to have distinct E/Z configurations about a C=C bond, which structural requirement must be met?
options: Two different substituents on each carbon of the double bond
Free rotation about the double bond
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Two different substituents on each carbon of the double bond

Each carbon of the double bond must have two different substituents. Restricted rotation about C=C then allows two distinct configurations. E/Z notation compares the higher-priority group on each carbon: together gives Z, opposite gives E. In simple examples such as but-2-ene, cis/trans terminology can also be used. If either carbon has two identical groups, there is no E/Z pair at that bond.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A triple bond: An ordinary carbon–carbon triple bond is linear and has only one external substituent on each carbon. It therefore does not create the two-sided arrangement required for an E/Z pair.

C. Free rotation about the double bond: Free rotation would allow the arrangements to interconvert easily. Rotation about a C=C bond requires disruption of π overlap, which creates the barrier separating its configurations. Ordinary single-bond rotation usually gives conformations rather than a stable alkene E/Z pair.

D. An asymmetric carbon: An alkene can have E/Z configurations without any tetrahedral chiral carbon. A carbon attached to four different groups is one common source of chirality, but it is not required for all enantiomerism either.

Key Educational Points:

  • Each double-bond carbon must have two different substituents for E/Z configurations to exist.
  • Restricted rotation results from the π interaction between the double-bonded carbons.
  • E/Z notation compares substituent priorities on the two carbons, not simply their sizes.
  • Cis/trans terminology works for familiar simple cases, while E/Z notation is more general.
  • Alkene stereoisomerism does not require a tetrahedral chiral carbon; substituted rings can also show cis/trans relationships.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: A molecule has one tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups and no other source of stereoisomerism. How many stereoisomers are possible?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 2

The four different groups around this carbon can form two configurations, designated R and S. These are nonsuperimposable mirror images, so they are enantiomers. With one such center and no other source of stereoisomerism, the count is two. The familiar 2ⁿ expression is an upper limit for n tetrahedral chiral centers when these are the only stereogenic elements; symmetry can reduce the count in molecules with multiple centers.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 1: One would mean only one distinct configuration. Here the four different groups create two nonsuperimposable mirror-image configurations. An achiral molecule still has a mirror image; its mirror image is simply superimposable on it.

C. 3: The specified single center has only two configurations, R and S, so there is no third configuration. Some molecules with multiple centers have three stereoisomers because of symmetry and a meso form, but that does not apply to this molecule.

D. 4: Four requires additional independent stereochemical variation, such as a second chiral center or a separate E/Z unit. The stem excludes those possibilities, leaving only two configurations.

Key Educational Points:

  • A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups is a common type of chiral center.
  • One such center, with no other stereogenic element, gives two configurations: R and S.
  • These two configurations are nonsuperimposable mirror images, called enantiomers.
  • Pure enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions under the same conditions; a racemic mixture has no net rotation.
  • For molecules whose only stereogenic elements are n tetrahedral chiral centers, 2ⁿ is an upper limit; symmetry can reduce the actual number.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which molecule can exhibit optical activity?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Butan-2-ol

Butan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃) has a chiral center at C2, bonded to four different groups: –H, –OH, –CH₃, and –CH₂CH₃. A sample containing more of one enantiomer than the other can rotate plane-polarized light; an equal mixture of the two enantiomers has no net rotation. The other molecules either lack four different substituents on any carbon (no chirality center) or are too symmetric.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Propan-2-ol: Propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃) has a central carbon bonded to –OH, –H, and two identical –CH₃ groups. Since two substituents are the same, this carbon is not a chiral center, so propan-2-ol cannot rotate plane-polarized light.

C. 2-methylpropan-2-ol: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol ((CH₃)₃COH) is a tertiary alcohol where the central carbon bears three identical methyl groups plus one –OH. With three of four substituents identical, there is no chiral center and no optical activity.

D. Methanol: Methanol (CH₃OH) is the simplest alcohol. Its carbon is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and one –OH group, giving it no chiral center. For a tetrahedral carbon to be a chirality center, its four attached groups must be different.

Key Educational Points:

  • Chirality means that a molecule is not superimposable on its mirror image. A pure enantiomer can show optical activity, whereas a racemate has no net rotation.
  • In butan-2-ol, C2 carries H, OH, CH₃, and C₂H₅ - four different groups, so it is a stereocentre.
  • For these alcohols, inspect each tetrahedral carbon for four different attached groups.
  • Check the whole structure as well: a molecule with stereocenters can still be achiral, as in a meso compound.
  • A racemic mixture of equal enantiomers also shows no net rotation, even though each molecule in it is chiral.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Meso-tartaric acid molecules are achiral despite having two stereocenters because they:
options: Have no chiral centers at all
Possess an internal plane of symmetry
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Possess an internal plane of symmetry

Meso-tartaric acid has an internal mirror plane in an appropriate conformation, making the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. It is therefore achiral despite having two stereocenters. A meso compound is a single achiral substance, whereas a racemate is an equal mixture of two different enantiomers.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Have no chiral centers at all: Meso-tartaric acid does have two stereocenters. The presence of stereocenters alone does not establish that the whole molecule is chiral; its overall symmetry also matters.

C. Are racemic mixtures: A racemate contains equal amounts of two enantiomers whose optical rotations cancel in the sample. Meso-tartaric acid is one achiral compound, so its lack of optical rotation does not require an enantiomer mixture.

D. Contain only one chiral center: Meso-tartaric acid has two stereocenters, not one. Its achirality follows from the relationship between the two halves of the molecule, rather than from an absence of stereocenters.

Key Educational Points:

  • A meso compound has stereocenters but is achiral as a whole.
  • Meso-tartaric acid illustrates how an internal mirror plane can make a structure superimposable on its mirror image.
  • A meso substance and a racemate are different: one is achiral, while the other contains two enantiomers in equal amounts.
  • Separating a racemate can give its individual enantiomers; a meso compound cannot be separated into an enantiomeric pair.
  • For a structure whose only stereogenic features are n tetrahedral centers, 2ⁿ is an upper bound; symmetry can reduce the number of distinct stereoisomers.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: When the atoms directly attached to a stereocenter are different elements, what determines their initial priority in the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) system?
options: Molecular weight of the entire group
Atomic number of the atom directly bonded to the chiral center
Number of bonds in the substituent
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Atomic number of the atom directly bonded to the chiral center

Compare the directly attached atoms first: the element with the higher atomic number has higher priority. For isotopes of the same element, the higher mass number takes priority, such as ²H over ¹H. If the directly attached atoms tie, compare the next sets of attached atoms in descending priority order and use the first difference.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Molecular weight of the entire group: The total molecular mass of a substituent is not the criterion. Compare atoms in sequence: for –CH₂OH and –CH₂CH₃, the first atoms are both carbon, but the next comparison includes oxygen versus carbon, so –CH₂OH ranks higher.

C. Electronegativity of the substituent: Electronegativity describes attraction for bonding electrons. It is not the ranking rule here: the initial comparison of different elements uses atomic number.

D. Number of bonds in the substituent: Simply counting bonds does not assign priority. Multiple bonds are represented using duplicate atoms when applying the comparison rules. Double and triple bonds are handled by the phantom atom rule: a C=O double bond is treated as if carbon is bonded to two oxygen atoms and oxygen to two carbon atoms.

Key Educational Points:

  • For directly attached atoms of different elements, higher atomic number means higher priority.
  • When directly attached atoms tie, compare the next attached atoms in descending priority order and stop at the first difference.
  • A double bond is treated as though the atom were duplicated.
  • Isotopes are an important exception to a simple atomic-number comparison: the isotope with the higher mass number ranks higher.
  • With the lowest-priority group pointing away from you, 1 to 2 to 3 clockwise is R and anticlockwise is S.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: A compound with the configuration (R)-2-bromobutane and its mirror image (S)-2-bromobutane are:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Enantiomers

Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that differ in the configuration at every chiral center. (R)-2-bromobutane and (S)-2-bromobutane are mirror images with opposite configurations at the single stereocenter. Enantiomers have the same ordinary physical properties in achiral environments, but opposite optical rotations under the same measurement conditions; they can interact differently with chiral substances.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Identical: The two structures have the same connectivity, but they cannot be superimposed: the four groups around C2 have opposite three-dimensional arrangements. They are different stereoisomers, rather than two drawings of the same configuration.

C. Diastereomers: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. Examples include E/Z alkene pairs and compounds differing at some, but not all, of several stereocenters. These two bromobutanes are instead a non-superimposable mirror-image pair.

D. Constitutional isomers: Constitutional (structural) isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity - for example, butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol. (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane have identical connectivity; they differ only in the 3D arrangement of atoms around the chiral center, making them stereoisomers (specifically enantiomers).

Key Educational Points:

  • Two molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers.
  • With a single stereocentre, inverting it produces the mirror image, so R and S forms of 2-bromobutane are an enantiomeric pair.
  • In achiral environments, enantiomers share ordinary physical properties; they can behave differently toward chiral molecules.
  • Diastereomers are not mirror images and generally have different physical properties, which can help separate them.
  • R/S is an assigned configurational label, not a measurement - it does not tell you which way the compound rotates light, which must be determined experimentally.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which statement about diastereomers is correct?
options: They are mirror images of each other
They are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images
They always have opposite optical rotations
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. They are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images

Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. They may differ at some of several stereocenters, or they may be E/Z alkene isomers. Their physical properties generally differ, so methods such as crystallization or chromatography can often separate them.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. They are mirror images of each other: Stereoisomers that are mirror images are called enantiomers, not diastereomers. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are specifically NOT mirror images. For example, (2R,3R)-tartaric acid and (2R,3S)-tartaric acid (meso) are diastereomers because they differ at one stereocenter but not all.

B. They have identical physical properties: Diastereomers are not required to have identical physical properties. Differences in properties such as melting point or solubility often allow separation by ordinary methods; this does not mean that every property must differ.

D. They always have opposite optical rotations: Pure enantiomers have equal and opposite optical rotations when measured under the same conditions. Diastereomers have no such predictable relationship - their optical rotations can differ in both magnitude and sign. There is no rule requiring them to be opposite.

Key Educational Points:

  • Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of one another.
  • Examples include structures differing at some of several stereocenters and E/Z alkene pairs.
  • Differences in physical properties often make diastereomers separable by ordinary laboratory methods.
  • Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images and have the same ordinary physical properties in achiral environments.
  • Cis-trans isomers are themselves a kind of diastereomer: stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The E/Z system for naming geometric isomers uses which priority rule?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules

The E/Z system assigns priorities to the two substituents on each carbon of the double bond using CIP rules, including atomic-number comparisons and the mass-number rule for isotopes. If the higher-priority groups are on the same side, the isomer is Z (zusammen, German for 'together'). If on opposite sides, it is E (entgegen, 'opposite'). This system is more general than cis/trans.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Alphabetical order of substituents: Alphabetical order does not determine E/Z priority. Apply the CIP rules separately at each alkene carbon, then compare the positions of the two higher-priority groups.

C. Molecular weight of substituents: The total molecular mass of a substituent does not determine E/Z priority. CIP compares atoms in sequence; when comparing isotopes of the same element, however, the higher mass number does give higher priority.

D. Size of substituents: Bulk alone does not set priority. For example, bromine outranks a group directly attached through carbon because Br has the higher atomic number, even if that carbon-containing group is much larger.

Key Educational Points:

  • The E/Z system assigns priority on each alkene carbon using CIP rules, exactly as R/S does at a stereocentre.
  • Z (zusammen, together) means the two higher-priority groups are on the same side; E (entgegen, opposite) means they are on opposite sides.
  • E/Z exists because cis/trans becomes ambiguous once the two carbons carry four different substituents.
  • Z is not simply a synonym for cis: the labels coincide only when the priority groups happen to be the ones cis/trans referred to.
  • CIP first compares atomic numbers, uses mass numbers to distinguish isotopes, and works outward to resolve remaining ties.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: How many stereoisomers exist for 2,3-dibromobutane?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 3

2,3-Dibromobutane has two chiral centers (C2 and C3). Normally, 2² = 4 stereoisomers would be expected. However, because the molecule has identical substituents on C2 and C3 (–CH₃ and –Br), one pair of configurations creates a meso compound (with an internal mirror plane). This reduces the total to 3 stereoisomers: (R,R), (S,S), and meso (R,S).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 2: Two chiral centers normally give 2² = 4 stereoisomers. However, 2,3-dibromobutane is a special case because the two halves of the molecule are identical. This creates a meso form (with an internal mirror plane) that reduces the count from 4 to 3: one (R,R), one (S,S), and one meso (R,S).

C. 4: The formula 2ⁿ = 2² = 4 gives the maximum possible stereoisomers for two chiral centers. However, because 2,3-dibromobutane has identical substituent patterns on C2 and C3, one pair of expected stereoisomers collapses into a single meso compound. This reduces the count from 4 to 3.

D. 5: Five stereoisomers is not possible from two chiral centers, since the maximum from 2ⁿ is 4, and the actual count can only decrease (due to meso forms), never increase beyond 2ⁿ. The correct answer is 3: a pair of enantiomers and one meso form.

Key Educational Points:

  • The 2ⁿ rule predicts 4 stereoisomers for two stereocentres, but 2,3-dibromobutane has only 3.
  • The two halves of the molecule are identical, so one combination possesses an internal mirror plane and is a meso compound.
  • The three are therefore one pair of enantiomers plus a single achiral meso form.
  • Always check for internal symmetry before applying 2ⁿ - it gives an upper limit, not a guaranteed count.
  • The meso form is a diastereomer of each enantiomer, so it differs in physical properties and can be separated from them.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Glucose is classified as:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: D. An aldohexose

Glucose is an aldohexose: it has six carbon atoms, and its open-chain form has an aldehyde at C1. In water it exists mainly as cyclic hemiacetals, but its classification still refers to the open-chain structure. Fructose is a ketohexose because its open-chain carbonyl is a ketone.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A ketopentose: A ketopentose is a 5-carbon sugar with a ketone (C=O) functional group. Ribulose is an example. Open-chain glucose has 6 carbons and an aldehyde group, so it is neither a pentose nor a ketose. Remember: “aldo-” = aldehyde at C1, “keto-” = ketone (usually at C2), “-pentose” = 5 carbons, “-hexose” = 6 carbons.

B. An aldopentose: An aldopentose is a 5-carbon sugar with an aldehyde group. Ribose (found in RNA) is a classic example. The open-chain form of glucose has an aldehyde but has 6 carbons, not 5, making it an aldohexose.

C. A ketohexose: A ketohexose has six carbons and a ketone in its open-chain structure, as in fructose. Open-chain glucose instead has an aldehyde at C1, so glucose is an aldohexose.

Key Educational Points:

  • Monosaccharides are classified by carbon count and by the carbonyl group in their open-chain form.
  • Open-chain glucose has six carbons and an aldehyde at C1, giving the name aldohexose.
  • Open-chain fructose has six carbons and a ketone at C2, giving the name ketohexose.
  • Aldoses are reducing sugars because the aldehyde can be oxidised; ketoses such as fructose still test positive, because alkaline test conditions isomerise them to aldoses.
  • The D in D-glucose refers to the configuration at the highest-numbered stereocentre (C5) relative to D-glyceraldehyde. It is a structural label and says nothing about which way the sugar rotates polarised light.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: The α and β anomers of D-glucose differ in the configuration at:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. C-1 (the anomeric carbon)

When glucose cyclizes to form the pyranose ring, the C1 aldehyde carbon becomes a new stereocenter called the anomeric carbon. In the usual Haworth drawing of D-glucopyranose, the α-OH is down and trans to the C6 CH₂OH group; the β-OH is up and cis to it. In the preferred ⁴C₁ chair, these hydroxyls are axial and equatorial, respectively; a chair flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions without changing α into β. Mutarotation involves ring opening and reclosing that interconverts the α and β anomers.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. C-2: C-2 is the carbon whose configuration distinguishes epimers like glucose and mannose (they differ only at C-2). The anomeric carbon in glucose is C-1, which is the carbon that forms a new stereocenter when the open-chain form cyclizes into the ring form.

B. C-4: C-4 configuration distinguishes glucose from galactose (they are C-4 epimers). Anomers specifically differ at the anomeric carbon (C-1 in aldoses like glucose), which is the hemiacetal carbon formed during ring closure.

D. C-6: C-6 is the terminal carbon bearing a –CH₂OH group in glucose; it is not a stereocenter in the ring form and plays no role in anomer formation. The anomers differ at C1: their OH groups are trans or cis to the C6 CH₂OH group, respectively, in α- and β-D-glucopyranose.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cyclisation turns the C1 carbonyl carbon into a new stereocentre, known as the anomeric carbon.
  • α and β anomers differ only in the configuration at that one carbon.
  • In the preferred ⁴C₁ chair of D-glucopyranose, the β-anomer's OH is equatorial; axial/equatorial is a conformation label, not the definition of α/β.
  • Anomers are diastereomers rather than enantiomers, because they differ at only one of several stereocentres.
  • Humans digest starch's α-linked glucose chains but lack cellulase for the β(1→4) linkages in cellulose.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Cellulose differs from starch primarily in:
options: The type of glycosidic linkage (α vs. β)
The number of carbon atoms per unit
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The type of glycosidic linkage (α vs. β)

Both cellulose and starch are polymers of D-glucose, but starch uses α-1,4 glycosidic bonds (and α-1,6 for branches), while cellulose uses β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Human amylases hydrolyze starch's α(1→4) linkages, and other digestive enzymes finish digestion, including at branch points. Humans lack cellulase for cellulose's β(1→4) linkages.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The monosaccharide units used: Both cellulose and starch are polymers of the same monosaccharide: D-glucose. The difference lies in how the glucose units are connected. Starch uses α(1→4) glycosidic bonds (easily digested by human amylase), while cellulose uses β(1→4) bonds (humans lack cellulase to break these, which is why we cannot digest cellulose/fiber).

C. The number of carbon atoms per unit: Both cellulose and starch are built from glucose, which has 6 carbon atoms per unit. The critical difference is the stereochemistry of the glycosidic bond: α in starch versus β in cellulose. This small geometric difference has enormous biological consequences for digestibility and structural properties.

D. The molecular weight: Both polymers have variable chain lengths and molecular masses. Their defining difference is linkage: starch contains α-linked glucose, whereas cellulose contains β(1→4)-linked glucose. The linkage changes chain shape and how enzymes recognize the polymer.

Key Educational Points:

  • Starch and cellulose are both polymers of D-glucose - they differ in the linkage, not in the monomer.
  • Starch uses α-1,4 bonds, with α-1,6 branches in amylopectin; cellulose uses β-1,4 bonds.
  • The β linkage flips alternate glucose units, producing straight chains that hydrogen-bond side by side into rigid fibres.
  • Human amylase acts on α(1→4) linkages in starch; cellulose requires cellulase, which humans do not produce.
  • Ruminants obtain cellulose digestion from gut microbes. Termites are not a valid example of animals universally lacking cellulase: they can use both their own enzymes and microbial enzymes.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Lactose is a reducing sugar because:
options: It has a free anomeric carbon on the galactose unit
It has a free anomeric carbon on the glucose unit
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. It has a free anomeric carbon on the glucose unit

Lactose consists of β-D-galactose linked β-1,4 to D-glucose. The glycosidic bond uses the C1 anomeric carbon of galactose, but the C1 of glucose remains free. This free anomeric carbon can open to form an aldehyde, which can reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent, making lactose a reducing sugar.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. It contains fructose: Lactose contains galactose and glucose, not fructose. Sucrose is the disaccharide that contains fructose (bonded to glucose). In lactose, galactose is linked through its C-1 anomeric carbon to C-4 of glucose, leaving glucose’s C-1 anomeric carbon free to open and act as the reducing end.

B. It has a free anomeric carbon on the galactose unit: In lactose, the galactose unit’s anomeric carbon (C-1) is involved in the β(1→4) glycosidic bond to glucose, so it is NOT free. It is the glucose unit that retains a free anomeric carbon capable of ring-opening to expose its aldehyde, which can then reduce Benedict’s or Fehling’s reagent.

D. Both anomeric carbons are free: Both anomeric carbons are not free in lactose. Galactose C1 participates in the β(1→4) linkage, while glucose C1 retains a free hemiacetal group and can open to the aldehyde form. That glucose end accounts for lactose's reducing behavior.

Key Educational Points:

  • Lactose is reducing because its glucose unit retains a free hemiacetal group that can open to an aldehyde.
  • In lactose the β-1,4 bond uses the anomeric carbon of galactose, leaving glucose's C1 free - hence it is reducing.
  • Sucrose is the contrasting case: its linkage ties up both anomeric carbons, so it is non-reducing.
  • Common free monosaccharides test as reducing sugars; fructose also reacts because alkaline conditions allow conversion to aldoses.
  • Benedict's and Fehling's tests detect reduction of copper(II); they are not specific tests for glucose or for an exposed aldehyde in the starting structure.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: D-glucose and D-mannose are:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Epimers differing at C-2

Epimers are diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one stereocenter. D-glucose and D-mannose have the same configuration at C3, C4, and C5, but opposite configuration at C2. D-glucose and D-galactose are C-4 epimers. Enantiomers would differ at every stereocenter (D-glucose vs. L-glucose).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Enantiomers: D-glucose and L-glucose are enantiomers: their corresponding stereocenters all have opposite configurations. D-glucose and D-mannose instead differ only at C2 and are not mirror images, so they are epimers.

C. Anomers: Anomers are cyclic sugar forms that differ specifically at the anomeric carbon (C-1 in aldoses) - the α and β forms of the same sugar. D-glucose and D-mannose differ at C-2 in their open-chain forms, so they are epimers, not anomers.

D. Identical compounds: D-glucose and D-mannose have the same molecular formula (C₆H₁₂O₆) but different configurations at C-2. They are clearly different compounds with distinct physical properties (different melting points, specific rotations). The term for sugars differing at exactly one stereocenter is epimers.

Key Educational Points:

  • Epimers are diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one stereocentre.
  • D-glucose and D-mannose differ only at C2; D-glucose and D-galactose differ only at C4.
  • Enantiomers, by contrast, require every stereocentre to be inverted - that is D-glucose versus L-glucose.
  • Epimers are different compounds, and enzymes can distinguish their different configurations.
  • Anomers are a special case of epimers: their configuration differs specifically at the anomeric carbon.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Mutarotation is the process by which:
options: The optical rotation of a freshly dissolved sugar changes over time until equilibrium between anomers is reached
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The optical rotation of a freshly dissolved sugar changes over time until equilibrium between anomers is reached

When a pure anomer of glucose (either α or β) is dissolved in water, the ring can open and reclose to form both anomers. This gradual interconversion causes the specific rotation to change over time until an equilibrium mixture is reached (approximately 36% α and 64% β for D-glucose at 25°C).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A sugar undergoes hydrolysis: Hydrolysis is the cleavage of a bond by addition of water, as when a disaccharide is split into monosaccharides. Mutarotation does not break any covalent bonds between sugar units - it is the interconversion between α and β anomeric forms of the same reducing sugar through the open-chain intermediate.

C. A sugar loses water: Losing water describes a dehydration or condensation reaction (like forming a glycosidic bond). Mutarotation involves the ring opening and reclosing of a single sugar molecule in aqueous solution, allowing the α and β anomers to equilibrate. The observed optical rotation gradually changes until the equilibrium mixture is reached.

D. A polysaccharide breaks down: Polysaccharide breakdown (hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds by enzymes like amylase) is a completely different process. Mutarotation refers specifically to the spontaneous change in optical rotation observed when a pure anomer of a sugar is dissolved in water, as it equilibrates between its α and β forms.

Key Educational Points:

  • Mutarotation is the change in observed optical rotation as a freshly dissolved sugar equilibrates between its α and β anomers.
  • It occurs because the ring opens transiently to the free carbonyl form and can reclose either way.
  • At equilibrium D-glucose is roughly 64% β and 36% α, with only a trace present as the open chain.
  • In the preferred chair of D-glucopyranose, the β-anomer has an equatorial anomeric hydroxyl, helping explain its greater abundance in water.
  • The rotation changes because the anomer ratio is shifting - the D/L configuration of the sugar is fixed and does not change.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which test can detect reducing sugars?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Benedict's test

On heating, reducing sugars reduce the blue Cu²⁺ in alkaline Benedict's reagent to copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O. Depending on the amount present, the result can range from green or yellow to orange or brick-red precipitate. Biuret, ninhydrin and xanthoproteic tests are used for different features of amino acids or proteins.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Biuret test: The biuret test detects proteins (peptide bonds), not sugars. It uses Cu²⁺ ions in strongly alkaline NaOH solution; when peptide bonds are present, they form violet-colored complexes with the copper. A minimum of two peptide bonds (i.e., a tripeptide or larger) is required for a positive result.

C. Ninhydrin test: The ninhydrin test detects free amino acids and primary amines. Most common α-amino acids give a purple-blue product, but proline, which has a secondary amino group, gives a yellow product. It is widely used in forensics (fingerprint detection) and amino acid analysis after chromatography.

D. Xanthoproteic test: The xanthoproteic test detects readily nitrated aromatic groups, especially those in tyrosine and tryptophan. Phenylalanine gives little or no color under usual test conditions. The test is used for amino acids or proteins, rather than to identify reducing sugars.

Key Educational Points:

  • Benedict's reagent detects reducing activity through Cu²⁺ reduction and formation of Cu₂O.
  • The observed color depends on the amount of reducing material and the test conditions; a positive result need not be brick-red.
  • Glucose, fructose, lactose and maltose react; intact sucrose ordinarily does not.
  • Fructose reacts after alkaline isomerization to aldoses, so an ordinary ketone group alone does not explain the result.
  • Benedict's test is not glucose-specific; iodine is the usual simple identification test for starch.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: At equilibrium in dilute aqueous solution near room temperature, free D-fructose predominantly adopts which ring size?
options: Both pyranose and furanose in equal amounts
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Pyranose (6-membered ring)

Under these conditions, the largest component is β-D-fructopyranose, approximately 70% of the mixture. Its six-membered ring forms when the C6 hydroxyl reacts with the C2 carbonyl to make a hemiketal. Smaller amounts of furanose forms and other forms are also present. The distribution depends on temperature and solvent; fructose within sucrose is instead locked into a furanose structure.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Furanose (5-membered ring): Five-membered fructofuranose rings are present in the aqueous equilibrium, and fructose has this ring size in sucrose. They are not the predominant free-fructose forms under the conditions in the stem.

C. Open-chain form: Only a small fraction is open-chain under these conditions. Most free fructose molecules are cyclic hemiketals; the open-chain form provides a route for interconversion between them.

D. Both pyranose and furanose in equal amounts: The ring forms do not occur in equal amounts. Near room temperature in dilute water, β-D-fructopyranose alone makes up roughly 70%; the proportions change with conditions.

Key Educational Points:

  • Free D-fructose in dilute water near room temperature is predominantly β-D-fructopyranose, with a six-membered ring.
  • The equilibrium proportions depend on temperature and solvent; one ring size is not universally preferred under every condition.
  • Fructose is often pictured as a furanose because that is the form locked in place within sucrose - the bound and free forms genuinely differ.
  • The ring-size names describe the ring itself: pyranose is six-membered and furanose five-membered, after pyran and furan.
  • Whichever ring forms, cyclisation generates the anomeric carbon and therefore allows mutarotation.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Saturated fatty acids differ from unsaturated fatty acids in that they:
options: Are always liquid at room temperature
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Contain no carbon-carbon double bonds

A saturated fatty acid has no carbon-carbon double bonds. For comparable chain lengths, a saturated chain usually packs more closely and has a higher melting point than a cis-unsaturated chain. The melting point also depends on chain length and other structural features, so saturated does not mean always solid.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Have shorter carbon chains: Chain length is independent of saturation. Both saturated and unsaturated fatty acids come in various chain lengths (commonly 12–24 carbons). For example, stearic acid (saturated, C18) and oleic acid (unsaturated, C18) have the same chain length but differ in saturation.

C. Are always liquid at room temperature: Saturated fatty acids are not always liquid or always solid at room temperature. Longer saturated chains often have relatively high melting points, whereas shorter ones can be liquid. Butter and oils are mixtures composed mainly of triacylglycerols, not simply samples of individual free fatty acids.

D. Are derived from plants only: Both plants and animals produce saturated and unsaturated fatty acids. Coconut oil and palm oil (plant-derived) are rich in saturated fats, while fish oils (animal-derived) are rich in unsaturated fats. The distinction is structural (presence of double bonds), not based on biological source.

Key Educational Points:

  • Saturated means no C=C bonds; monounsaturated means one and polyunsaturated means two or more.
  • Cis double bonds bend the chain and usually lower melting point compared with a saturated chain of similar length.
  • Chain length and double-bond geometry also matter; physical state cannot be inferred from saturation alone.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: A triglyceride is formed by esterification of:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Glycerol with three fatty acids

A triglyceride, or triacylglycerol, has all three hydroxyl groups of glycerol esterified with fatty acid residues, which may be identical or different. In the formal reaction between glycerol and three free fatty acids, three water molecules are released. Triglycerides are the main form of fat storage in the body and the primary component of dietary fats and oils.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Glycerol with one fatty acid: Esterification of glycerol with only one fatty acid produces a monoglyceride (monoacylglycerol), not a triglyceride. Monoglycerides are important emulsifiers used in food processing and are also intermediates in fat digestion.

B. Glycerol with two fatty acids: Glycerol bonded to two fatty acids forms a diglyceride (diacylglycerol, DAG). DAG is a signaling molecule in cells and an intermediate in both triglyceride synthesis and breakdown. A triglyceride (“tri-” = three) specifically requires all three hydroxyl groups of glycerol to be esterified with fatty acids.

D. Sphingosine with three fatty acids: Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids (such as sphingomyelin and ceramide), not triglycerides. Triglycerides are built on a glycerol backbone. Sphingosine is a long-chain amino alcohol, structurally different from glycerol, and sphingolipids play important roles in cell membranes and signaling.

Key Educational Points:

  • Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups, allowing formation of three ester bonds.
  • Mono-, di- and triacylglycerols contain one, two and three fatty acyl groups, respectively.
  • Triacylglycerols are major energy-storage lipids; their three fatty acid residues need not be the same.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Saponification of a fat produces:
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Soap (fatty acid salts) and glycerol

Saponification is base-promoted hydrolysis of a triacylglycerol with NaOH or KOH. It yields glycerol and fatty acid carboxylate salts, which are soaps. Three hydroxide ions are consumed per triacylglycerol overall. For a triacylglycerol with identical acyl groups: triacylglycerol + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3RCOONa.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Fatty acids and glycerol: Acidic hydrolysis gives glycerol and free fatty acids. Under saponification conditions, the products are instead carboxylate salts because the reaction occurs in base and consumes hydroxide overall.

C. Fatty acids and ethanol: Ethanol is not a product of fat saponification. Glycerol (a triol with three –OH groups) is released when the three ester bonds of the triglyceride are cleaved. Ethanol would appear in ester hydrolysis only if the original ester were an ethyl ester, not a glycerol ester.

D. Fatty acid esters and water: The ester bonds are being broken, not formed. With aqueous NaOH, the overall reaction consumes hydroxide and yields glycerol plus sodium carboxylates; ester and water are not the products.

Key Educational Points:

  • A triacylglycerol contains three ester bonds that can be hydrolyzed.
  • Saponification produces glycerol and fatty acid salts, rather than free fatty acids under the basic reaction conditions.
  • Hydroxide is consumed overall: saponification is base-promoted, not simply catalyzed by a regenerated base.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Which lipid class forms the main bilayer framework of human cell membranes?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Phospholipid

Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate-containing region and hydrophobic regions that favor bilayer formation in water. Many are glycerophospholipids, with glycerol and two fatty acyl chains. Sphingomyelin is also a phospholipid, but has a sphingosine-based backbone. Cholesterol and proteins are important additional membrane components.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Triglyceride: Triglycerides are the main form of energy storage in adipose tissue. They are predominantly hydrophobic (three nonpolar fatty acid tails, no polar head group) and cannot form the bilayer structure needed for membranes. Phospholipids, with their polar head and two nonpolar tails, are amphipathic and spontaneously form bilayers.

B. Cholesterol: Cholesterol is an important membrane component that modulates fluidity - it prevents membranes from becoming too rigid at low temperatures or too fluid at high temperatures. However, cholesterol inserts between phospholipids; it is not the primary structural building block of the bilayer itself.

D. Wax: Waxes are esters of long-chain fatty acids and long-chain alcohols. They commonly provide protective surface coatings, rather than forming the phospholipid bilayer of human cell membranes. Their extreme hydrophobicity makes them unsuitable for forming the dynamic bilayer structure membranes require.

Key Educational Points:

  • Amphipathic lipids contain both water-attracting and water-avoiding regions.
  • In a bilayer, polar heads face water and hydrophobic chains face the interior.
  • Glycerophospholipids and sphingomyelin illustrate that phospholipids need not share the same backbone.

chemistry.subject: chemistry
chemistry.question: Cholesterol belongs to which class of lipids?
chemistry.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Steroids
